TIDE is the shared platform under the Runink applications. This guide covers what an admin or a developer needs to operate it. It describes what ships.
The documentation has five sections, one per console category, plus the agent model cards:
OverviewSign in, the console map, the architecture, and every HTTP route. DevExThe core CLI, coding sessions, the agent fleet, reviews, CI workflows, and the cluster pages. DataExModels and inference, connections, runners, trust and access, data governance, judgements. IntelligenceCapEx, rule governance, Resolve, playbooks, Ask, audits and lineage. FORGEThe Studio, forge.yaml, central verification, and the /forge/ contract. Model cardsOne card per agent: what it reads and produces, its model, what a person approves, and its limits.
data.how-each-section-is-organised#How each s: Getting started: a guided first pass over the category’s pages. Task and concept pages: how one part works, with the names you will meet in the console and the code. Reference: routes, RPCs, commands, triggers and settings, derived from the source. Troubleshooting: real error messages, quoted from the code, with their cause and fix.

DataEx is the console category for the people who consume what the platform decides. It covers which models serve, which agents act and within what limits, how the model plane is used, which tenant sources Runink TIDE reads and what reads them, what TIDE may do and who may do it, and the independent verdicts on findings.
The rail order: Agents · Models & inference · Connections (Connections, Runners) · Trust (Harness, Autonomy, Access, Judgements); Admin is in the rail footer, under the instance row. Model cards and Inference are one page, Secrets & PKI is a sub-tab of DevEx › Cluster › Namespaces, and the Model & agent audit verdict is on the Overview’s audit strip.
Quick startFrom an empty console to a first data audit, using a fictional company you can download. Getting StartedA tour of every DataEx page, with its ?tab= name and the endpoint behind it. ConnectionsThe connection wizard, the registry API and core connection register. Data-access runnersThe Runink managed runner, enrolling a self-hosted runner, and the refusal codes. Models & inferenceModel cards, the inference plane and the model router’s admission queue. Trust & accessAdmin allowlists, Harness, guardrails, Secrets & PKI and the Admin page. Data governanceThe datagov agent’s controls, verdicts and what it never reads. JudgementsThe judgement contract: one document, two write doors, three outcomes. API ReferenceDataEx HTTP routes, their auth class, and the gRPC services behind the pages. TroubleshootingReal error strings from the console and the CLI, with cause and fix.
data.three-rules-that-hold-across-dataex#Thre: Reads never dial. No DataEx page load contacts a tenant source. The one path that dials a registered source is Resolve’s action RPCs (Test, Explore, Access patterns, Map estate). They run in the console process, only on an admin’s action. See Resolve. Credentials are write-only. A connection’s credential bundle is stored separately from its record. No read returns it. Unread is never empty. When the console cannot read a source it says so in the body (source:"unavailable", complete:false, an unmeasured[] entry with the reason). It does not report “none”.

Every route below is registered in registerRoutes and served by the console on the same origin as the Flutter app. The auth class of each was checked in its handler.
Auth classes
session: a console session cookie (requireSession). Without one the answer is 401 {"error":"unauthorized"}. admin (LIST): a session plus adminRefusal against that allowlist. The answer is 403 with the refusal sentence. See Trust & access. App token: a bearer GitHub App token carrying the App’s rights for the console’s org (authorizeReporter). A missing bearer is 401 {"error":"missing bearer token"}. ingest token: a shared machine secret. Unset means the door refuses everything. Most report GETs answer 200 even when their source is unreadable, and say so in the body (source:"unavailable", complete:false, unmeasured[]). GET /api/connections and GET /api/runners are the exceptions. Both answer 503 with the report in the body.

Omitting credentials keeps the stored bundle /api/providers GET session cloud-provider config (GCP/AWS/Azure) and the connectors Runink TIDE publishes /api/providers POST admin (CORE_CONNECTION_ADMINS) merge by section /api/providers/gcp/status GET session the live GCP fleet link (opt-in) /api/connectors/status GET session the cached connector probe. The pages use the gRPC services below.

Here the runner is the gRPC server and TIDE is the client.
Service RPC What RunnerBootstrapService Enroll (bidi stream) TIDE sends EnrollChallenge, the runner sends EnrollProof (its proof, a CSR and its version), TIDE sends EnrollIssued (server leaf and runner CA), and the runner sends EnrollInstalled. The token is consumed only after both proofs verify RunnerService Health the runner measuring itself. It never touches a source RunnerService Renew a CSR over a fresh keypair RunnerService InstallCertificate hand over the renewed leaf. The old one is then refused RunnerService Goodbye why TIDE is dropping the runner. data:
A connection is a record in Runink TIDE’s console registry. It says which external system a tenant’s data lives in, where it is, and which credential bundle unlocks it. The registry is the store/connections package, opened by the console.
TIDE’s records are TIDE’s own. TIDE and the apps share the store/connections package, but each holds separate records. Nothing syncs, mirrors or reconciles TIDE’s registry with an app’s.
data.connectors-tide-publishes-not-registry-r: The platform’s own connectors are configured under POST /api/providers (connectors[]) and published to the connectors. They are not registry records, so Resolve cannot test them. GET /api/connectors/status never dials: it returns the last cached probe, and a connector that was never probed is NOT MEASURED. Only POST /api/connectors/status/refresh dials, and it is admin-write under CORE_CONNECTION_ADMINS. The types with a probe are databricks, snowflake, mqtt, rfid, sensorgateway, gps, and the REST systems oms, tms, wms, yms, ims and whs. A type with no probe is reported measured:false. POST /api/providers merges by section: an absent or null key keeps what is stored, and "connectors": [] clears it.
data.create-a-connection-in-the-console#Creat:
DataEx › Connections (?tab=connections) is the only place to create, edit, test and rotate connections. It is the shared datasources wizard (ConnectionsService).
Pick a source card. Cards map to types in the connector catalog. A card whose type the catalog lacks is shown as unavailable. Fill the settings the type reads. Enter credentials in their own step. Credentials are write-only: no read ever returns them. Choose the runner that will reach the source. Runink managed is stored as "" (the console process itself). A self-hosted runner is stored by name. See Data-access runners. Save, then Test. Test is Resolve’s Test, run through the shared estate server on the connection’s bound runner. It is the one dialler, and there is no fallback runner. Every change, Test and Verify goes through the handler’s own allowlist: CORE_CONNECTION_ADMINS for connection changes, and CORE_ATLAS_ADMINS for Test and Verify, because those dial the source. Every attempt is written to the audit chain. See Trust & access.
Resolve’s Add credentials and the onboarding wizard’s Add source open this same wizard.
data.keeping-secrets-out-of-the-manifest#Keep:
The CLI screens every manifest client-side before it writes:
Structural. Unknown fields are parse errors, and a settings key must be a setting that the console’s catalog says the connector reads. Credential screening. Keys and values are screened for credentials that belong in the credential bundle instead, before and after ${VAR} expansion. What the screen looks for is deliberately not published: a published list tells a reader exactly what it does not catch. Names, not values. The bundle is assembled from environment variable names at apply time. No error message echoes a value. Every write is read back and compared.
data.manifest-format#Manifest format:
A host or an account locator is a fact about one installation’s estate, so keep a real manifest in the repository that owns that estate.
apiVersion: runink.org/partner-connections/v1 partner: template # groups the file; documentation only description: >- … connections: - id: template-replace-this-id # plain identifier: names a credential file name: TEMPLATE — replace this type: postgres # must be in the TARGET console's catalog environment: replace-me settings: host: ${TEMPLATE_POSTGRES_HOST} port: 5432 # never a ${VAR}: numeric settings are refused as strings database: ${TEMPLATE_POSTGRES_DATABASE} username: ${TEMPLATE_POSTGRES_USERNAME} ssl_mode: require properties: owner: ${TEMPLATE_POSTGRES_OWNER} credentials: - key: username fromEnv: TEMPLATE_POSTGRES_USERNAME - key: password fromEnv: TEMPLATE_POSTGRES_PASSWORD ${NAME} resolves inside settings and properties only, from the environment, at apply time. An unresolved reference blocks the connection, which is why applying the template unedited writes nothing. A credential entry has exactly key and fromEnv. The YAML is decoded with KnownFields(true), so a value: line is a parse error. Declare an ownership property, such as owner or steward, so the data governance agent can name who owns the source. Prefer an ssl_mode of require, verify-ca or verify-full: prefer and allow can fall back to plaintext.
data.register-connections-from-a-manifest#Reg:
core connection register applies a committed manifest through the console’s own /api/connections:
export CORE_CONSOLE_URL=https:// export CORE_CONSOLE_SESSION= # or CORE_CONSOLE_USER + CORE_CONSOLE_PASSWORD export MY_POSTGRES_HOST=… MY_POSTGRES_PASSWORD=… # from your secret store core connection register my-estate.yaml --dry-run Flag Effect --dry-run validate and report what would happen, writing nothing --adopt-drift overwrite a console connection whose settings differ from the manifest (off by default: an edited connection is a decision) --rotate-credentials replace the credential bundle of a connection that already exists (off by default, because saving REPLACES) The console URL comes from --console-url or CORE_CONSOLE_URL. There is no default. It must be https unless the host is loopback. The session (CORE_CONSOLE_SESSION, or CORE_CONSOLE_USER + CORE_CONSOLE_PASSWORD) is read from the environment only, never from core.yaml.
data.the-json-registry-api#The JSON registry:
These routes stay available for one release as deprecated aliases. core connection register still posts to them.
Route Method Auth /api/connection-types GET session. The connector catalog: the settings and credential keys each type reads /api/connections GET session. Lists records. Answers 503, with the full report in the body, when the registry is unreadable /api/connections POST admin-write, CORE_CONNECTION_ADMINS /api/connections/{id} GET session. 404 no connection with id when absent /api/connections/{id} PUT, DELETE admin-write, CORE_CONNECTION_ADMINS The write body (connectionWrite) is id, name, type, environment, runner, config, properties, credentialRef and credentials. On an update, omitting credentials leaves the stored bundle untouched. The body is capped at 256 KiB. A nested id such as a/b is refused rather than truncated, because the id names a file in the credential store.
The type is canonicalised on write, so Service Now, service-now and servicenow all store as one type. An unrecognised type is stored as-is, because the catalog is a known-types table, not a closed set.
data.the-report#The report:
State Meaning CREATED nothing was there. The record is written, with its bundle if one was declared UNCHANGED the same connection exists. It is not rewritten DRIFTED a different connection exists. The differing fields are printed, nothing is written, and the exit code is 1. --adopt-drift overwrites ADOPTED a drifted connection was overwritten because --adopt-drift was given BLOCKED a declared credential or ${VAR} is unset. Nothing is written, and the missing variable names are printed Drift is decided before rotation. The console’s PUT writes the record and the bundle in one call, so rotating a drifted connection would adopt the drift.
Two columns are deliberately not answers:
NOT CHECKED: registration establishes nothing about reachability, and there is no --verify and must not be one. The CLI never dials. TIDE’s only connector runtime is the console’s Resolve, on an admin’s action, so use Resolve’s Test. NOT REPORTED: whether a bundle is present. Answering that writes a GET_CREDENTIALS audit record per connection.

This page walks the DataEx rail from top to bottom. For each page it gives the label, the ?tab= name for a deep link (/?tab=), and the endpoints the page reads.
Rail label ?tab= What it reads Agents agents GET /api/agents, GET /api/swarm, GET /api/agent-config, GET /api/access, GET /api/guardrails Models & inference inference GET /api/models, plus GET /api/agents for its inference.router block Connections connections the shared ConnectionsService (gRPC-web); each row also carries what Intelligence › Sources showed (/api/domains, /api/connectors/status, WorkspaceService grants, Resolve), with Sources’ sections below the list Trust harness tabs Harness (GET /api/harness), Autonomy (?tab=guardrails, GET /api/guardrails), Access (?tab=policy, GET /api/access), Judgements (?tab=judgements, GET /api/judgement, GET /api/judgements) Connections carries Runners as its second tab (?tab=runners, the shared RunnersService). Admin (the shared AccessService) is in the rail footer, under the instance row, and only for an admin of the chosen instance.
Old links still land: ?tab=modelCards opens Models & inference, ?tab=sources opens Connections, ?tab=runners opens Connections on Runners, ?tab=guardrails, ?tab=policy and ?tab=judgements open Trust on Autonomy, Access and Judgements, ?tab=secrets and ?tab=security open DevEx › Cluster › Namespaces on Secrets & PKI, ?tab=modelAgentAudit opens the Overview with that audit’s panel open, and ?tab=measures goes to Harness.
data.agents#Agents: The console’s agent roster (GET /api/agents) lists every agent, including the core session CLI. Each card carries the agent’s purpose, trigger, delivery (workflow, cli or cronjob), model tier and the gate that arms it. The page also shows each app agent’s live health (/api/swarm), its ini settings and OpenBias rules (/api/agent-config, read from each repo’s HEAD), who may arm agents (/api/access) and the hard guardrails (/api/guardrails). The fleet itself is documented under DevEx › Agent fleet.
data.connections#Connections: This page is where tenant data-source connections are created, edited, tested and rotated. It is the shared datasources wizard. Credentials are write-only, and Test is Resolve’s Test run on the connection’s bound runner. See Connections.
data.inference#Inference: The model router and per-tier usage and quotas. See Models & inference.
data.judgements#Judgements: The docket of findings that external assessment platforms have submitted, and TIDE’s own verdicts on them. See Judgements.
data.model--agent-audit#Model \u0026amp; agen: An assessment page, not the audit log. It reaches one verdict over the six reads listed above: model health against each card, OpenBias coverage per app agent, the autonomy guardrails, the Harness’s open findings and the independent judgements. Its actions go through the paths that already exist. A Harness action stays on Trust › Harness, and the judge agent is started through an existing playbook (PlaybookService.RunNow).
data.model-cards#Model cards: One row per serving tier. Each row joins three sources: the reviewed model card, what the tier is actually running, and the latest inference bench when a measurement can be attributed to that tier. A tier is healthy only when it is deployed, is ready, has not just been OOM-killed, and runs the model its card names. More in Models & inference.
data.runners#Runners: The data-access runners: the built-in Runink managed runner (console) and any self-hosted runners Runink TIDE connects out to. These are not CI runners. See Data-access runners.
data.trust#Trust: Harness: the console’s own findings (from /api/measures and /api/compliance), each with only the actions TIDE can really take. An admin’s POST to /api/harness/{id}/act runs one. Guardrails & autonomy: an autonomy level of off, hitl or auto for each action class. The default is hitl, and every act is taken by a signed-in admin. Policy & ReBAC: which allowlists are set, how large each is, and your own membership. Admin: the members and seats of the instance chosen on the landing page. Secrets & PKI: the shared mesh CA as distributed to each namespace, with its subject, SHA-256 fingerprint and validity window. See Trust & access.
data.where-to-go-next#Where to go next: Register a source on Connections. Explore it on Intelligence › Resolve, so that the datagov agent can assess data quality and PII exposure. Read the result in Data governance.

data: The datagov agent assesses the tenant’s registered data sources. It is deterministic and calls no model: a model-authored governance score would be a fabrication wearing a number. It holds no credential, dials no source, and reads no row or cell value.
data.controls#Controls:
The agent groups its controls into four axes. Each control gives one verdict per connection, with the reason:
Axis What it covers governance whether the connection says who owns it and which environment it belongs to, whether its type is one the connector catalog describes, and whether its credentials are its own and kept out of its ordinary settings risk-compliance whether the connection declares where it reaches, keeps credentials out of that address, and protects the transport data-quality (from Resolve’s Explore) whether what a source declares about its own structure agrees with what was measured, and whether its tables are keyed pii-exposure (from Resolve’s Explore and access patterns) whether columns that may hold personal data are masked, and how widely such data can be read What each control looks for is deliberately not published. A published list of the exact keys, patterns and thresholds a check uses tells a reader precisely what it does not catch. The console shows every finding, with its reason and the column paths involved, to the people who can act on it. A source nobody has explored gets one unable-to-assess per axis, saying “not explored yet — run Explore in Intelligence › Resolve”. To fill the two data axes, Explore the source on Resolve.
The personal-data findings are a starting point for review, not a guarantee that every sensitive column was found.
data.not-the-same-as#Not the same as: compliance: checks Runink TIDE’s own code against its control index. risk: govulncheck over dependencies. judge: judges findings submitted by other platforms. See Judgements.
data.verdicts#Verdicts: pass, fail, warn and unable-to-assess. The last one is the point: a control the agent cannot evaluate is never shown as satisfied or omitted, and it always carries the reason.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The connection snapshot: a copy of the connection table that the console publishes after every write. This covers the governance and risk-compliance axes. What Resolve’s Explore recorded, read from the console with the agent’s own app token. It holds structure and counts only: names, declared types, nullability and primary keys, row and null counts with their basis, the source’s PII flag and mask, and access counts. This covers the data-quality and PII-exposure axes. The agent reads it from the console on purpose, rather than from a published copy: a description is the tenant’s schema, so it stays sealed at rest in the console.
data.when-it-runs#When it runs: daily at 07:11 UTC; on an @core_datagov issue comment; on a manual run of the agent’s workflow; when an Atlas playbook step names datagov. Arm or disarm it with the gate agentic_datagov from DataEx › Agents.
data.where-the-results-land#Where the results: The console findings store: the agent writes its findings to the console with its app token, and signed-in users read them there. Findings name column paths so an owner can act. The living GitHub issue, “🗃️ Data governance status”. It carries counts only, so the tenant’s schema stays on the platform. A successful store write raises the harness event findings.reported (fail_count, warn_count), which can start a matching Atlas playbook. See Playbooks. Tests hold the value boundary: no finding carries a setting value or a cell value, and what Explore hands the agent carries no values.

data:
A judgement is Runink TIDE’s independent verdict on a finding that an external assessment platform submitted. The judge agent makes it and lands it on the finding in the console’s store. The page is DataEx › Judgements (?tab=judgements).
The docket starts empty. CORE_JUDGEMENT_INGEST_TOKEN gates POST /api/judgement/submissions, and while it is unset the endpoint refuses everything. An admin issues it when an external assessment platform is onboarded. Until then the judge reports unable-to-judge, with that reason. That is the design working, not a bug.
data.not-the-same-as#Not the same as: eval’s judge scores our own agents’ run traces 0..1 against a golden set. judge assesses somebody else’s finding against its evidence. The plan gate in fixer, selfheal and triage runs the same checks over each agent’s own proposal before it acts.
data.one-document-three-routes#One document,:
The console owns the shape: a store with version, revision, updatedAt, submitters{} and judgeRuns[]. Its source of truth is the console’s own table, and the copy the agent reads is rewritten after every change, so make changes in the console. The agent reads that copy and defines nothing.
The routes are split by authority, never by a field in the body:
Route Method Authority What it does /api/judgement[?submitter=NAME][&batch=ID] GET browser session the submitted findings and TIDE’s verdicts on them. Answers 200 even when the store is unreadable, and says so in the body /api/judgement/submissions POST the submitter’s shared CORE_JUDGEMENT_INGEST_TOKEN as a bearer findings in. Any verdict on the wire is discarded, because a platform may not grade its own work. The response is the stored, judged batch. Re-posting the same batchId is idempotent. The body limit is 1 MiB /api/judgements POST the GitHub App’s rights for the console’s org (authorizeReporter) verdicts in, from TIDE’s own judge agent. This is the only way a verdict enters the store /api/judgements GET browser session the judge agent’s runs The ingest token is refused by name at the judge’s door: “the submission ingest token has no authority here: a platform that submits findings does not judge them.”
data.outcomes#Outcomes:
concur, dissent or unable-to-judge (the console also accepts its own out-of-scope). Anything else is refused at the door. Unable-to-judge is never rendered as agreement. When the judge cannot reach a verdict it abstains, with the reason.
Deterministic checks run before any model call. A quantitative claim is settled by arithmetic over the evidence’s own numbers, never by a model, and a claim the evidence contradicts is a dissent. The model sees only what arithmetic cannot settle, and is never told the submitter’s stance. How the judge weighs evidence beyond that is deliberately not published: a public description of exactly what passes would be a recipe for submissions written to pass it.
Every verdict carries a stable reason code. Two of them matter operationally:
blocked-by-guard is a block, not an outage. The guardrails withheld the claim or the model’s answer, so a person reviews it. The judge reports it in its own “Blocked by guard” section, never retries it and never counts it as agreement. model-unavailable is the only retryable reason: a later run may judge that submission again.
data.the-fast-path#The fast path: Before its LLM call, the judge may answer with a small pinned tree model, switched by the Actions variable CORE_FAST_JUDGEMENT (default on). It answers only the clear cases, and never without evidence. Whatever it does not answer goes to the LLM exactly as before. Every model-based verdict records which path it took, for example basis: model (fast-model judgement-fast v0 sha256:…) or model (llm).
data.when-the-judge-runs#When the judge runs: daily at 08:29 UTC; on an @core_judgement comment; on a manual run; as a playbook step. It writes to two sinks: the console store and the living “⚖️ Judgement status” issue. A successful store write raises the harness event judgements.reported (dissent, unable).

data: Everything on the model plane is sovereign. It serves the platform’s own models on its own engine, and there is no hosted-model path. mistral.rs is the engine.
data.budgets-come-from-one-rate#Budgets come: Every model-calling agent derives its max_tokens and timeouts from one configured decode rate, INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S (the inference library’s DecodeRateEnv). The default is 3.4 tok/s, an estimate for CPU-only server hardware, to be measured with the inference bench. The platform decodes one request at a time, so a 2000-token answer is roughly ten minutes of pure decode. Size budgets from the rate, never from wall-clock intuition, and never from a developer workstation.
data.inference-tabinference#Inference (\u003c:
The Inference page reads GET /api/models and the inference.router block of GET /api/agents. GET /api/inference remains the plane as deployed: engine and version (from the image reference; :latest is reported as :latest, not as a version), running digest, model and quantization (from --quantized-file/--model-id), context window, device, requests and limits, live memory and CPU, ready/desired, restarts and last termination.
An empty context window means the engine default was taken. That is a finding, not a blank. Live usage is absent, not zero, when no metrics source is available. When metrics.k8s.io does not exist, the console reads the kubelet Summary API through the apiserver node proxy and labels the source kubelet-summary. A 403 is unmeasured, never zero.
data.model-cards-tabmodelcards#Model cards (\:
GET /api/models (session-gated) returns one row per serving tier, joined from three sources:
Source What it gives card the reviewed model card, embedded in the console: provenance, licence, pin, intended use, scope, evaluation evidence live the same tier projection /api/inference renders: model, quantization and context from the container spec; ready, restarts, last termination and digest from the pods; memory from metrics.k8s.io bench the latest inference bench, attached only when the measurement can be attributed to that tier The health verdict is the join. A tier is healthy only if it is deployed, ready, not just OOM-killed, and running what its card names. A tier that serves happily from the wrong weights is not healthy. Live memory at or above 90% of the limit is degraded (modelMemoryWarnPct).
Usage is reported only as far as it exists:
Token use comes from the app agents’ own /api/agent-health reports. It is cumulative since each agent process started, and is neither a time series nor per tenant. Per-tenant compute allocation is ClientInstance.spec.computeUnits, a sizing budget. Billed model time is measured separately, in slot milliseconds, by the model router (below); see Plans and billing. Admission, queue depth and token quotas are not exported by anything. They appear as unmeasured[] entries.
data.the-model-router-cmdmodelrouter#The mode:
One OpenAI-compatible front door that sends each request to the backend of the tier its model field names. It is also the one admission queue in front of the engines: the engines decode a bounded number of requests at a time, and the router decides which request is served next.
What a caller can rely on:
Work waits rather than fails. When every slot is busy, a request queues. When the router cannot serve it in time, it answers 503 with Retry-After instead of holding it indefinitely. The two messages are modelrouter: inference queue full; retry later and modelrouter: no inference slot within ; retry later. A caller that leaves takes its work with it. A request that is still queued is dropped before the engine sees it, and one in flight is aborted, so the slot is freed for someone who is still waiting. A caller can say how long it will wait, and the router never queues work past that deadline. People are served ahead of background work. A request made for a person waiting in the console goes ahead of agents and schedulers, and that priority cannot be claimed without proof: the console signs those requests with a key the TIDE operator mints, and an unsigned claim is ignored. Background work is never starved, and nothing is refused for lack of priority. Tiers that cannot be substituted are not. A request for a tier with no backend of its own either falls back to the general tier (coder and vision) or is refused (embedding and voice), because a chat model returns no usable vectors or audio. GET /status reports, per backend, the queue and the wait it can promise. It orders only traffic that goes through it. The router’s configuration lives in the deployment manifest. Its admission and scheduling internals are not documented here: they are the platform’s own, and they change with measurement.
The ops doctor and the inference bench deliberately call the engine directly: the doctor must not depend on a hop it reports on, and the bench measures the engine itself.

From an empty console to a first data audit, using a fictional company you can download. No vendor account, no customer data, nothing to invent.
This page follows the console’s own Start here panel on the Overview. Those five steps are read from the platform — connect a source, test it, map the estate, run an audit, invite a member — and are never ticked by hand. When this page says a step is done, the console will say so too, because both are reading the same thing.
Apply the sample systems only to a test instance, never to a production deployment. They are stand-ins with weak, published credentials: a Kafka with no authentication, a PostgreSQL whose password is in the manifest, a Guidewire stand-in with a published login, an RTSP camera with no credentials at all. Use a scratch machine or a scratch cluster.
data.step-1--connect-a-data-source#Step 1 — C:
Download the bundle for the source you want and create the connection from DataEx › Connections › New connection.
# one connection type curl -LO https://docs.runink.org/downloads/connections/postgres.zip # or the whole set, with checksums curl -LO https://docs.runink.org/downloads/connections/SHA256SUMS curl -LO https://docs.runink.org/downloads/connections/manifest.json Each zip holds that platform’s schema in its own idiom, the synthetic rows, and the model TIDE should discover from it. That last part is what makes this testable rather than a showcase: you can compare what the console mapped against what the bundle says it should have mapped.
Twenty-five types ship as zips. The other seven — cctv, gps, iot, kafka, mqtt, rfid, sensorgateway — are streaming connectors, so a zip is the wrong shape for them. They ship as replays instead:
curl -L https://docs.runink.org/downloads/connections/streams/mqtt/manifest.json A full inventory of both, with a sha256 per file, is in manifest.json , and universe.json describes the whole company. The download folder has no directory listing, so start from the manifest.
Credentials are write-only. The console never returns one after it is stored; rotating is a separate action. Every placeholder in these bundles is change-me — the publisher refuses to ship anything else, along with any non-documentation IP, any host outside .invalid, and anything over 25 MiB.
data.step-2--test-the-connection#Step 2 — Tes:
Test on the connection row. It is not a ping: it is Resolve’s Test run on the connection’s bound runner, so it answers “can the thing that will actually read this reach it?” rather than “is the hostname spelled right”.
A fresh console has only the built-in Runink managed runner (console). That is enough for every bundle here. Self-hosted runners are for sources TIDE must reach inside your network — see Data-access runners.
Until a source answers a test, the Overview says so in as many words: “None of your N sources has answered a test yet.”
data.step-3--map-the-estate#Step 3 — Map the:
Mapping walks each connected source and records what is in it — datasets, fields, and the domains it infers from them. The Overview then reads “N datasets mapped from M sources”, counted from the platform rather than from this page.
This is the step where the shared identifiers start paying: the same SHP-50004 in a TMS, a WMS, a telematics feed and a claim file is what lets the next step reconcile across them instead of auditing each in isolation.
data.step-4--run-the-first-data-audit#Step 4:
The audit is what the six anomalies are for. A run that finds none of them has not failed politely — it has not read the data, and that is worth chasing rather than accepting.
Until one has run, the Overview is explicit: “No data audit has run yet.”
data.step-5--invite-a-member#Step 5 — Invite: The last step exists because an audit nobody can open is an audit nobody acts on. Admin is in the rail footer, under the instance row, and appears only for an admin of the chosen instance.
data.what-stands-up-locally#What stands up lo: A synthetic fixture is data, not a running system. The FACE quickstart grades say, for every type, whether it stands up locally or needs a vendor account.
data.what-you-are-about-to-connect#What you a:
One fictional logistics company — Quillmere Freight Lines (quillmere.invalid) — written out in the native shape of every connection type the catalogue offers. The same shipment, order, carrier, claim, SKU and device identifiers appear across all of them, so cross-source reconciliation actually lines up instead of being asserted.
It carries six planted anomalies. They are the point of the bundle, not decoration — each one is a thing TIDE and FACE should find, and each spans more than one source. In broad strokes they cover:
freight billed above its contracted rate; a claim at risk of missing its filing window; a cold-chain temperature excursion; one customer order fulfilled twice; a vehicle off its planned route; goods received that no shipping notice accounts for. This page does not spell out the exact values or how each is detected. The bundle’s expected model says what a correct reading finds, so you can check the console’s result against it.
data.where-the-bundles-come-from#Where the bu: The bundles are generated from one deterministic source, and every download is checked against a fresh generation before it is published, so the files you download and the expected models agree.

A data-access runner is the process that dials a tenant source on Runink TIDE’s behalf. It is not a CI runner; GitHub Actions runners are a separate thing.
The page is DataEx › Runners (?tab=runners).
Resolve actions and CapEx pulls run on the Runink managed runner (console). A self-hosted runner enrols, connects and reports its health. An action routed to it is answered with runner_offline and the detail “connected; …”, and nothing runs. Choose console for the action.
data.address-grammar#Address grammar: host:port, where the host is an IPv4 address, a [bracketed] IPv6 address or an RFC 1123 DNS name, and the port is 1–65535. The console refuses URL schemes, userinfo (@), IPv6 zone ids, unbracketed IPv6, the unspecified and multicast addresses, and anything that looks like a credential.
data.choosing-the-runner-per-action#Choosing:
Every Resolve action and CapEx PullFeed accepts an optional runner:
absent: use the connection’s binding, whose empty value is console; console: Runink managed, explicitly, even for a connection bound to a self-hosted runner; a name: that runner, with no fallback. The runner is picked at audit time on Intelligence › Data audit. A connection’s default binding is set in the Connections wizard with the same picker. The effective runner and whether it was “chosen for this action” or “the connection’s binding” are recorded in the audit detail.
data.copy-the-ticket-which-is-shown-once#Copy: The ticket is crt1. followed by base64url of the enrolment ticket: the token, the runner id and name, the expiry, and the runner CA’s SHA-256. It carries no endpoint. It is valid for 15 minutes, works once, and enrols only this runner. TIDE stores only the token’s SHA-256, and holds the enrolment proof key in memory only. If the console restarts before the runner is reachable, issue a new token.
data.create-the-runner#Create the runner: Add runner on the page, or POST /api/runners {name, address, zone, labels}. The name is a DNS label. The response is {runner, ticket, command}. The runner starts PENDING.
data.enrol-a-self-hosted-runner#Enrol a self-: You must be allowed by CORE_RUNNER_ADMINS. When it is unset, every signed-in identity is allowed.
data.operating-a-runner#Operating a runner: Action Route Notes Health polled every 15 s (RunnerService/Health) every figure is a runner claim and is labelled so. Health never touches a source Renewal automatic before a third of the leaf’s life is left, TIDE asks for a CSR over a fresh key, records it as the NEXT fingerprint, installs it, then promotes it. The old leaf is then refused Edit address PATCH /api/runners/{id} audited with the old and new address. The certificate stays valid. A zone or label change on a PENDING runner revokes its live token New ticket POST /api/runners/{id}/token PENDING runners only. The old token is revoked Revoke token DELETE /api/runner-tokens/{id} an unused token Revoke runner POST /api/runners/{id}/revoke sends Goodbye(REVOKED) best-effort and never dials again. The runner writes revoked and exits 0 GET /api/runners is session-gated and never dials. For each runner it serves id, name, displayName, kind, address, zone, labels, state and health.{connected, lastSeen, version, certNotAfter, inFlight, limit}. Each runner also reports its concurrency limit, and whether that limit is enforced. An unreadable registry answers 503, never “only console”.
data.refusal-codes#Refusal codes:
None of them opens a credential bundle or calls the engine, and none falls back to another runner:
Condition Outcome name not registered runner_unknown runner REVOKED runner_revoked runner PENDING runner_offline (not enrolled yet) ACTIVE, not connected runner_offline ACTIVE and connected runner_offline, detail “connected; …” registry unreadable failed, “runner registry unavailable” (never runner_unknown)
data.runners-tide-deploys#Runners TIDE deploy: TIDE can provision a runner itself: on an on-premise host over SSH, or on a Compute Engine VM in your GCP project. The ticket is handed over inside the target. Deploying is admin-only with a stricter rule than the rest of the page: an unset CORE_RUNNER_ADMINS refuses everyone. Credentials are referenced by id under CORE_DEPLOY_SECRETS_DIR//, never typed.
data.start-the-runner-on-its-host#Start the r: CORE_RUNNER_TICKET='crt1.…' core-runner serve --listen :7443 The ticket goes in the environment. A ticket on the command line is refused, and the variable is unset as soon as it has been read. core-runner flags: --listen (env CORE_RUNNER_LISTEN, default :7443) and --state-dir (env CORE_RUNNER_STATE_DIR, default /var/lib/core-runner, mode 0700). A runner that TIDE deployed reads its ticket from CORE_RUNNER_TICKET_FILE instead. That file must be regular and 0600 or 0400, and setting both variables is refused.
data.the-two-kinds#The two kinds: Kind on the wire Display What it is managed Runink managed, id console the console process itself. It is never stored and is synthesized on every read. It can never be revoked, re-addressed or enrolled. self_hosted the name you gave it a core-runner process on a host you run, stored as kind enrolled in the registry (var/lib/core-runners) Registry limits: 100 runners, 100 tokens, 8 labels per runner, and a 512 KiB budget. Writes over a limit are refused, never truncated.
data.tide-dials-the-runner#TIDE dials the run:
TIDE connects out to each self-hosted runner at the address an admin entered. There is no runner listener, port, DNS record or devgateway pass-through on TIDE’s side, and no CORE_RUNNER_ENDPOINT. The link is mutual TLS on the runner CA, a separate trust root from the mesh CA. The TIDE operator mints it once. Identity is the certificate, never the address, so IPv4, IPv6 and FQDN addresses all work, and changing an address is only a reconnect.
If your installation’s pod network is IPv6 single-stack, a runner must be reachable from the console pod over IPv6, an AAAA FQDN, or NAT64.
data.tide-enrols-it#TIDE enrols it:
TIDE dials the address, then retries with backoff. Connect now (POST /api/runners/{id}/connect) tries at once. Both sides prove they hold the token with an HMAC bound to that TLS connection’s exporter, so a relay fails. The runner sends a CSR for a key it just generated. TIDE signs a 24-hour runner server certificate that names only spiffe://core.runink/runner/, with no DNS or IP name, and consumes the token in one step. The runner is ACTIVE.
State on the runner host: identity.pem (certificate and private key, 0600), ca.pem and runner.json, key.pending.pem (present only during an enrolment or renewal), and revoked (written on revocation, after which the runner refuses to start).
data.what-a-runner-never-does#What a runner n: It holds no source configuration and no stored credentials, schedules nothing, and its Health never touches a source.

data: Every message below is quoted from the source named beside it. Placeholders in angle brackets stand for values the console fills in.
data.connections#Connections: the connection registry is not configured on this console, or GET /api/connections answering 503 The registry did not open at boot. The console log says connection registry unavailable — /api/connections will report it. The usual cause is that the console cannot resolve CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK: store/connections seals unconditionally and refuses to open without it. no connection with id (404) A stale id, for example from a cached list. Reload the page. expected /api/connections/{id} (404) The path is nested (a/b). Ids are plain identifiers, because each id names a credential file.
data.core-connection-register#\u003ccode\u003: no console named: pass --console-url or set CORE_CONSOLE_URL. There is no default console, by design. console URL "" must be https: this request carries your console session AND the credential bundle this manifest declares Use https. Only loopback hosts may be plain http. no console session: set CORE_CONSOLE_SESSION to an existing … cookie value, or set CORE_CONSOLE_USER and CORE_CONSOLE_PASSWORD … Export one of these. Neither is read from core.yaml. the console at has no password sign-in configured (CONSOLE_ADMIN_PASSWORD is unset there); use CORE_CONSOLE_SESSION with a session cookie instead The console only offers Google sign-in. Copy a session cookie instead. the console at could not issue a session (its session store, appfs core-console/run/sessions, is unavailable) … This is a server-side fault, and no client setting can work around it. Fix the console’s session store. connection "" has type "", which this console's connection catalog does not describe … The type is not in the target console’s catalog (GET /api/connection-types). The message lists the described types. connection "": settings[""] is not a setting the connector reads, and this console would drop it silently rather than refuse it. Use the setting names the catalog reports. The message lists them. fromEnv is required — it is the NAME of the environment variable the credential is read from A credential entry needs fromEnv, and a value: field is a parse error. BLOCKED in the report A declared credential or a ${VAR} is unset or empty. Nothing was written. Export the named variables. DRIFTED, exit code 1 The console’s record differs from the manifest. It was probably edited in the console. Decide which side is right, then re-run with --adopt-drift if the manifest wins.
data.judgements#Judgements: judgement submission is not configured (CORE_JUDGEMENT_INGEST_TOKEN unset), so this endpoint accepts nothing (503) No submitting platform has been onboarded yet. Until an admin issues the token, the judge reports unable-to-judge. bad ingest token (403) The submitter’s bearer does not match CORE_JUDGEMENT_INGEST_TOKEN. the submission ingest token has no authority here: a platform that submits findings does not judge them. … (403) A submitter’s token was presented at POST /api/judgements. Only Runink TIDE’s judge agent, with the GitHub App token, may post verdicts. token does not carry the App's rights for org "" The agent’s bearer is not an installation token or user token of TIDE’s GitHub App for this org. this console does not know its GitHub org: the TIDE GitHub App names no installation it can read and CORE_GITHUB_ORG is unset … Mount the App key or set CORE_GITHUB_ORG. Every App-token door (/api/judgements, /api/data-governance-*, /api/session-runs) refuses until one of them is present.
data.model-plane#Model plane: modelrouter: inference queue full; retry later or modelrouter: no inference slot within ; retry later (503 with Retry-After) The plane decodes one request at a time. Wait for the Retry-After. Model-calling agents already wait out a 503 inside their own window. modelrouter: no backend configured (503) BACKEND_ is unset for an embedding or voxtral request. Those tiers have no general fallback. A model card shows a tier as unhealthy while it serves The verdict requires the tier to run what its card names. Compare the card’s pin with the live model in GET /api/models.
data.runners#Runners: the runner CA is not available on this console: — … Enrolment is disabled until the runner CA exists and is mounted. The core-operator mints it on its first reconcile; let it reconcile. Never regenerate the CA: every runner would have to re-enrol. address "" … — enter host:port, where host is an IPv4 address, a [bracketed] IPv6 address or a DNS name Remove any scheme (://), userinfo (@) or zone id. Bracket IPv6 addresses, and use a port from 1 to 65535. a runner named "" is already registered Runner names are unique. Pick another. runner "" is pending and TIDE holds no live ticket for it (expired, used, revoked, or the console restarted since it was issued) — issue a new token The 15-minute ticket lapsed, or the console restarted, because the proof key lives in memory only. Choose New ticket and restart core-runner with it. runner "" is already enrolled; a token enrols a PENDING runner only — revoke it and enrol a new one to replace it Tokens exist only for pending runners. runner "" is revoked and can never enrol again — enrol a new runner Revocation is permanent. Enrol a new runner with a fresh state directory. the built-in "console" runner cannot be revoked — it is this console process (§4) Runink managed has no lifecycle. core-runner: refusing a ticket on the command line — argv is readable by every local user; pass it in CORE_RUNNER_TICKET (cmd/core-runner) Put the ticket in the environment. core-runner: both CORE_RUNNER_TICKET and CORE_RUNNER_TICKET_FILE are set; give the ticket one way Unset one of them. the ticket file is readable by group or others (mode …); it must be 0600 or 0400 Run chmod 600 on the file. A Resolve action or CapEx pull ends runner_offline with “connected; …” The runner is connected. Resolve actions and CapEx pulls run on the Runink managed runner: choose Runink managed (console) for the action. runner_unknown, runner_revoked, or failed “runner registry unavailable” See the refusal table in Data-access runners. None of them falls back to another runner.
data.sign-in-and-permissions#Sign-in and perm: {"error":"unauthorized"} (401) There is no valid console session. Sign in again. If nobody can sign in, check the boot log for the next entry. 🛑 CONSOLE SIGN-IN DISABLED — a sign-in method is configured but the session store (appfs core-console/run/sessions) cannot be mounted … Sessions live in the console’s appfs root. Check CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK and the OBJECTSTORE_* / CONSOLE_APPFS_DIR wiring. The mount is retried on the next sign-in. is not permitted to change connections on this console (CORE_CONNECTION_ADMINS) (adminRefusal) The allowlist is set and does not name you. The same shape appears with CORE_RUNNER_ADMINS, CONSOLE_AGENT_ADMINS (“act on harness findings”) and the other lists. Ask an admin to add you. GET /api/access shows which lists are set and whether you are on each. this console has no sign-in configured, so a connection change would be unattributable — set GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID or CONSOLE_ADMIN_PASSWORD before storing or removing tenant credentials Writes are refused outright on an open console. Configure a sign-in method. Runners have the equivalent message: “…a runner enrolment or revocation would be unattributable…”. no verified console identity on this request (adminRefusal) The session carries no verified email. Sign out and sign in again.

data: The Trust sub-section of DataEx holds Harness, Guardrails & autonomy, Policy & ReBAC, Admin and Secrets & PKI. This page also covers the rule under all of them: how the console decides who may change something.
data.admin-tabadmin#Admin (\u003ccode\u003e?t:
The members and seats of the instance chosen on the landing page, over the shared AccessService. The rail draws it only when the server says you are an admin of that instance, and every access RPC re-checks the role. An admin is a spec.users entry with role admin on that instance’s live ClientInstance (expiry honoured), or CORE_PLATFORM_ADMIN. It is never one of the console capability lists above: those administer the console, not an instance’s membership.
Changes are a JSON merge patch of the whole spec.users array, carrying the CR’s resourceVersion. A raced patch is therefore refused rather than silently undone. A change is reported PENDING until the operator re-projects the app’s users and the app rolls. Seats go through the billing seat RPCs in-process. The ui component’s rules: nobody changes their own access, the last admin stays, and a full seat pool refuses an invite.
data.guardrails--autonomy-tabguardrails#Guard:
GET /api/guardrails (session) and PUT (admin, CONSOLE_AGENT_ADMINS). The page sets an autonomy level per action class, optionally per domain: off (refused), hitl (a human clicks) or auto. Everything defaults to hitl. Levels are stored in the console’s harness-guardrails table and audited before the store is written. Hard guardrails, drawn from rules the platform already enforces, cap a finding at hitl or refuse it, whatever the level.
Every act is taken by a signed-in admin. TIDE runs no unattended executor, whatever the level: auto is recorded, and every response states how acts are executed (autoExecution). The same payload carries modelGuardrails: the model-call guardrails, read from the console’s one guardrail instance. The console refuses to start if it cannot be built. What the guardrails look for is deliberately not published: a published list tells a reader exactly what they do not catch. /chat and Ask screen what a person typed before any model call, and screen the model’s text before it is shown or acted on.
data.harness-tabharness#Harness (\u003ccode\u:
GET /api/harness joins /api/measures (the platform’s self-assessment) and /api/compliance (per-control findings) into one list of findings. Each finding offers only actions TIDE can really take:
Action class Executor dispatch_agent repository_dispatch to a named agent workflow, with the console’s App installation token file_issue a tracking issue in the agents repo carrying the evidence needs_human an acknowledgement, recorded An agent that addresses a domain but that the console cannot start is shown as an unavailable action with the reason.
POST /api/harness/{id}/act runs one, in this order:
Session plus CONSOLE_AGENT_ADMINS. The finding must be live now. The guardrail level must not be off. An idempotency reservation: a repeat within the window replays the earlier result. Audit before act: if the intent record is not durable in the chain, nothing happens and the answer is 503. Act, then record the outcome.
data.machine-ingest-tokens#Machine-ingest tok:
Agents and apps do not use sessions. Each machine door takes a shared secret generated once in core-system by the provisioner, projected optional: true, and refusing everything while unset:
Env Door CORE_HEALTH_INGEST_TOKEN app agents’ POST /api/agent-health CORE_RECON_INGEST_TOKEN the recon agent’s POST /api/rules-recon/report and GET /api/rules-recon/inputs CORE_ROUTER_IDENTITY_KEY the model router’s check that a request was made for a signed-in person CORE_JUDGEMENT_INGEST_TOKEN POST /api/judgement/submissions. Issued when an external platform is onboarded; see Judgements TIDE’s own agents report with a GitHub App installation token for the console’s org instead (authorizeReporter). That covers /api/data-governance-findings, /api/data-governance-estate, /api/judgements, /api/session-runs and the playbook doors.
data.policy--rebac-tabpolicy#Policy \u0026amp:
GET /api/access (session, read-only) renders the table above live. For each list it reports whether the list is set and its size, and only your own membership. It also lists every ClientInstance with a count of admin, writer and reader grants and your own role, and whether CORE_PLATFORM_ADMIN is configured.
Access is decided by the allowlists above and by each instance’s per-person roles.
data.secrets--pki-tabsecrets#Secrets \u0026am: GET /api/security reports the shared mesh CA certificate as distributed to each platform namespace: subject, SHA-256 fingerprint, notBefore/notAfter and days remaining. Use it to confirm that the root is identical across namespaces and to catch an expiring CA. The mesh leaves rotate in-process and are never stored, so the CA is the artifact to inspect. The page degrades to source:"unavailable" when the CA has not been distributed anywhere reachable. The “Model guardrails” rail on this endpoint is read from the Guard, never from env.
data.sign-in#Sign-in:
A session requires a configured sign-in method: GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID (Google) or CONSOLE_ADMIN_PASSWORD (password). Who may sign in:
CONSOLE_ALLOWED_EMAILS: an address list. This is the console’s own variable, not the apps’ AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS. CONSOLE_ALLOWED_HD: a hosted e-mail domain, consulted only when CONSOLE_ALLOWED_EMAILS is unset. With neither set, nobody may sign in (fails closed). Sessions are server-side, in the console’s appfs root (run/sessions). /auth/logout revokes the current session. If the session store cannot be mounted (usually a missing CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK or an unreachable objectd), the console logs CONSOLE SIGN-IN DISABLED at boot and refuses every sign-in.
data.the-privileged-write-rule#The privileged:
A GET is session-gated (requireSession). A write that changes who is trusted, what runs or what is provisioned also passes one predicate, adminRefusal, and is audited on success, failure and refusal:
No sign-in configured: the write is refused outright (403), because nobody could be attributed. No verified identity on the request: no verified console identity on this request. The allowlist is set and does not name you: is not permitted to on this console (). The allowlist is unset: every identity this console admits is allowed. That is not a wildcard, because sign-in itself already fails closed. Allowlist (optional keys in the console’s Secret) Governs Unset means CONSOLE_AGENT_ADMINS arming agents, acting on Harness findings, changing guardrails, and POST /api/github every signed-in operator CORE_CONNECTION_ADMINS the connection registry, POST /api/providers, connector probe refresh every signed-in operator CONSOLE_INSTANCE_ADMINS the /chat tools that mutate (create_client_instance) every signed-in operator CORE_ATLAS_ADMINS Atlas gRPC-web writes, including Resolve’s dialing actions and connection Test/Verify every signed-in operator CORE_RUNNER_ADMINS enrolling, re-addressing, connecting and revoking data-access runners, and their tokens every signed-in operator. Exception: deploying a runner refuses everyone while unset CONSOLE_SESSION_ADMINS ending another person’s sessions and reading the audit trail nobody (everyone may still end their own) CONSOLE_SESSION_ADMINS is the odd one out: it only seeds this installation’s metastore on first boot. After that, the list is edited through GET/PUT /api/session-admins (DevEx › Session admins). CORE_PLATFORM_ADMIN names the installation’s platform admin, whom the operator makes admin on every instance.

data:
DevEx is the console category for the people who build and run the platform. It covers what is deployed and how traffic reaches it, whether git is the source of truth, whether the audit record is intact and who may read it, whether the CI plane’s watcher is alive, and what the agents did. This section also covers the tooling behind those pages: the core CLI, Runink TIDE’s own coding agent (core session), the agent fleet, and the GitHub Actions workflows that run it.
Getting StartedBuild the CLI, run the dev stack, run a first coding session. CLI ReferenceEvery core command and flag, taken from the binary’s own –help. data: Runink TIDE runs its own agents on its own model. The console roster (GET /api/agents) lists eighteen: compliance, curator, datagov, deployer, eval, fixer, hunter, judge, opsdoctor, recon, reviewer, risk, selfheal, triage, resolver, forger, users and session. Each agent is built from source per run, with no third-party SDK.
data.behaviours-worth-knowing#Behaviours wort: opsdoctor must never become a workflow. It heals the CI plane, so it cannot depend on it. It is the only agent that ships as an image. compliance proposes and cannot apply. Its workflow holds contents: read. datagov holds no credential and dials nothing. It assesses data quality and PII exposure only from what Resolve’s Explore recorded, read from the console. A source nobody explored stays unassessable. See Data governance. judge abstains rather than agreeing. Its outcomes are concur, dissent and unable-to-judge. Submissions are accepted once CORE_JUDGEMENT_INGEST_TOKEN is set. See Judgements. recon calls an ungoverned rule Shadow, so a fresh workspace is mostly Shadow. That is by design. A model failure is loud. reviewer, triage and selfheal post a degraded notice when the model is unreachable instead of exiting green.
data.managing-schedules-from-the-console#Mana: GET /api/agent-schedules lists fleet cadence and enablement, and which of it is editable. PUT /api/agent-schedules/{name} arms or disarms an agent with a body carrying at least one of enabled, dryRun or schedule. It is a privileged write gated by CONSOLE_AGENT_ADMINS and audited. In the console this is Agent runs › Runs, “Schedules & arming” tab (?tab=agentSchedules).
data.models-and-budgets#Models and budgets:
Agents use the general model unless told otherwise; the reviewer and fixer use the coder model. Every model-calling agent goes through the model router, the one front door to the engines. The exceptions are deliberate: the ops doctor must not depend on the hop it reports on, and the inference bench measures the engine itself.
Agent cost is decode-seconds, not runner-minutes. The model plane serves one request at a time. Every budget derives from one configured rate, INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S. It defaults to 3.4 tok/s and is set as an Actions variable of the same name. Each agent derives its token budget from its deadline rather than declaring it separately. At that rate a 2,000-token answer is about ten minutes of pure decode.
Size budgets from the deployment target, not the dev workstation. The 3.4 tok/s default is an estimate for CPU-only server hardware; measure yours with the inference bench.
data.pairs-that-look-like-duplicates-and-are-: Pair The boundary curator security audit vs risk The curator reads first-party code committed since its last run (CWE/OWASP, model-judged). risk runs govulncheck over dependencies (known CVEs, reachable). curator compliance audit vs compliance The curator starts from a diff and asks which controls it touches. compliance starts from the control index, checks every citation still exists, and deep-reads three controls. selfheal vs opsdoctor selfheal needs a job that ran and failed. opsdoctor sees jobs that never run and runner pods that crash, from a CronJob outside Actions. selfheal vs the apps’ self-healing The agent diagnoses failing CI runs. The apps’ self-healing restarts, isolates or rolls back an app. judge vs eval’s judge eval scores our agents’ run traces against a golden set. judge assesses someone else’s finding against its evidence.
data.started-by-atlas-playbooks#Started by At: Six agents can be started by a playbook step: datagov, compliance, risk, judge, recon and curator. Each runs only when the step names it, and reports its outcome back to the playbook run. A curator started by a playbook is treated exactly like the scheduled run. See Playbooks.
data.switches#Switches:
Variable (Actions variable of the same name) Default Effect CORE_FIXER_JUDGEMENT, CORE_SELFHEAL_JUDGEMENT, CORE_TRIAGE_JUDGEMENT on the shared plan gate judges the agent’s own proposal before it acts. Only off, false, 0, no or disabled turns one off CORE_FAST_JUDGEMENT on the judgement fast path runs in front of the LLM for judge and the three plan gates CURATOR_CRON_DRY_RUN unset means dry the scheduled curator publishes only when this is the literal string false CORE_FORGE_ENABLED off arms the forger With the plan gate, a dissent blocks the action. The fixer pushes nothing and reports unresolved, self-heal posts a “withheld” notice, and triage posts the classification with labels withheld. Unable-to-judge does not block: the fixer’s draft is titled [not verified by the judge], and self-heal and triage say NOT VERIFIED. Every run prints a line beginning PLAN-GATE: (off, empty, concur, dissent or unable) with the tally.
A green curator run proves nothing. A dry run does everything except publish and then finishes green, and an unset CURATOR_CRON_DRY_RUN means dry.

data:
What each DevEx page in the console shows, the endpoint it reads, and the rules that endpoint keeps. Every /api/* GET here needs a console session.
How to read absence. These endpoints answer 200 even when they could not read a source, and say so in the body (source:"unavailable", complete:false, or an unmeasured[] list with the API’s own reason). An empty list means “none”; an unreadable one is reported as unmeasured, never as empty.
data.audit-chain--get-apiaudit-get-apiauditse:
The console’s hash-chained audit log, persisted in its appfs root at var/log/audit and continued across restarts.
GET /api/audit returns a newest-first page and the chain’s verdict. Filters: actor, action, outcome (success, denied or failure), since (RFC 3339 or a duration such as 24h), limit, before (a chain seq). GET /api/audit/{seq} returns one record in full with its neighbours’ hashes. Records carry seq, at, actor, action, target, outcome, detail, hash, prevHash. GET /api/audit/verify walks the persisted chain and names the first record that was edited, removed, inserted or reordered. 200 with ok:false is a detected break; 503 means there is no persisted chain to check. Only session admins may read the trail, and the check fails closed. It is cross-identity data: sign-ins, refused sign-ins, revocations, and who armed which agent.
data.doctor--get-apidoctor#Doctor — \u003ccod: Traces agents/opsdoctor, which is a k8s CronJob rather than a workflow so that it keeps working when the runner pool it watches is dead. It shows the CronJob’s state (present, SUSPENDED, schedule, last run times), its recent Jobs and how they ended, and the tracking issue (label ops-doctor) with the time of the last report. Suspension is surfaced first, because a benched doctor looks exactly like a healthy quiet one.
data.gitops--get-apigitops#GitOps — \u003ccod:
The response has one of two modes:
mode: "argo": the Argo CD Application list could be read. It shows sync and health per Application. mode: "github-actions": Argo CD is absent and delivery runs as a workflow. Per workload: desired is the newest delivery lineage record that planned or rolled the workload: commit, image, digest, run, time and roll verdict; running is the pods’ imageID digests and the placement labels on the live object (app.kubernetes.io/version, runink.org/commit); drift is decided on the digest when the build reported one, else on the commit label. It is null when neither pair was read, never false. The commit stamp. The delivery roll makes one strategic-merge kubectl patch of the pod template. It sets the label runink.org/commit= and the annotation kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt, and re-pins every container on the node-local registry to :latest@. If the patch cannot be built or is refused, it falls back to a plain rollout restart with a ::warning.
Because of the stamp, CD-rolled workloads are digest-pinned. A bare kubectl rollout restart restarts onto the same digest. To move a workload onto new images, run the delivery workflow for that image. “Did my commit ship?” is Deploy lineage (GET /api/lineage?sha=), on the Intelligence rail. See Data audit & deploy lineage.
data.instances--get-apidashboard#Instances —: The tenant instances (ClientInstances) with app, tenant, role, phase, readiness and endpoint, plus the FinOps attribution projected from the CR (initiative, compute units, tier, expiry).
data.metrics--get-apimetrics#Metrics — \u003c:
Measured process and workload metrics only. They come from this process (runtime and /proc) and the live API server. There is deliberately no uptime percentage and no network throughput, because the process cannot measure either. Every block carries a source.
Live CPU and memory come from metrics.k8s.io when it exists. When it is absent (as on a single-node k0s install), they come from the kubelet Summary API through the apiserver node proxy, labelled source: "kubelet-summary". That needs nodes/proxy get on the core-operator ClusterRole. A 403 is reported as unmeasured, never zero.
data.namespaces--get-apinamespaces#Namespaces:
For every tracked namespace plus every tenant client-* namespace, it shows the admission posture (PSA labels, NetworkPolicies), the workloads (Deployments, DaemonSets, StatefulSets) with ready/desired, their pods (restarts, node, why the last container died), Warning events, and ResourceQuota/LimitRange. Each namespace closes with one verdict and the sentence that justifies it. A “Nodes & placement” sub-tab covers nodes; GET /api/nodes/{name} inspects one node.
Container logs are not read, by design: they can carry secrets, and the operator’s ServiceAccount has no pods/log grant.
data.platform-audit#Platform audit: An assessment page, not the audit log. It gives one verdict over checks read from existing endpoints: /api/audit/verify, /api/gitops, /api/doctor, /api/metrics, /api/reviews, /api/compliance and /api/governance-runs. A check that could not be read goes into a not-measured list, never counted as a pass. Its only actions are the ones the console already has: re-verify the audit chain, and start a review through an existing playbook’s PlaybookService.RunNow.
data.reviews--get-apireviews-get-apireviewsty:
What each review found, per type:
Type Runs from Findings from code run store: reviewer, fixer, resolver open PRs labelled review:findings-open risk run store: risk the “🛡️ Dependency risk report” issue compliance run store: compliance /api/compliance plus the “📋 Compliance status” issue headline dataQuality run store: datagov, plus datagov assessments and CapEx scan runs the datagov findings store and the CapEx findings dataConsistency CapEx scan runs the CapEx “Consistency” control dimension aiMaturity, dataMaturity none, computed on read /api/maturity A run whose findings were not recorded carries summary: null and findingsStored: false with the reason, never a zero count that would read as a clean review. /detail adds what the agents posted on GitHub.
data.routing--get-apiroutes#Routing — \u003cc:
How traffic reaches each service, and whether the thing it reaches is serving. The routing table is the DEVGW_ROUTES env var on the devgateway DaemonSet, plus the console’s own /forge/ path. The table’s origin is reported as:
Origin Meaning pod read from a running devgateway pod, so it is what routes right now daemonset read from the DaemonSet template, so it is what the next pod gets declared the committed manifest, used only when the edge could not be read. No route with this origin is called “serving”
data.runs--get-apiruns#Runs — \u003ccode\u003:
One history of every autonomous agent run, whatever started it. It is a view over stores that already exist:
Kind Source workflow agents the run store, all repos it holds, topped up through /api/agent-runs’ staleness gate pipelines the run store’s pipeline runs CLI sessions the session-report table and your own command queue CronJobs the batch Jobs of opsdoctor and the platform’s maintenance CronJobs (no log: pods/log is not granted) app agents /api/agent-health, latest only The “Schedules & arming” tab reads GET /api/agent-schedules. See Agent Fleet.
data.session-admins--getput-apisession-admins:
Who may read the audit trail and end another person’s sessions. The list is a document in this installation’s metastore (var/lib/session-admins), not a manifest value:
CONSOLE_SESSION_ADMINS in the console’s Secret is the first-boot seed only. Once the document is written, changing the Secret changes nothing. Unset means nobody, unlike the other admin lists. PUT replaces the list. It refuses an empty list, and one that drops the caller unless someone else remains. Every attempt is audited, and a change is made durable in the audit log before it is written. A console with no sign-in configured refuses: this console has no sign-in configured, so no identity can be a session admin.

data.check-the-cli#Check the CLI: core --help Config resolves from ./core.yaml or ~/.core.yaml, then CORE_* environment variables, then flags (see CLI Reference).
data.deploying-to-a-cluster-instead#Deploying: core dev is the local run loop. Deploying to k0s is a different layer: core deploy platform|face|pulse|all with --mode local (multipass VMs) or --mode onhost (a single-node k0s on the host itself). See CLI Reference.
data.get-portless-urls-one-time-sudo#Get port: core dev hosts # map *.runink.org.local → 127.0.0.1 and grant the gateway :443 core dev secure # optional: add the single mTLS SNI gateway The success banner ends with TIDE dev up (envelope + pipe-mesh + rotating raft mTLS + eBPF + diagnostics/MCP + self-heal). followed by the per-app URLs. The TIDE console runs as a shell only (/api/* needs the operator and a cluster).
data.run-a-first-coding-session-safely#Run a: core session start --repo / \ --prompt "Summarise the README, then call done" \ --dry-run --dry-run runs the full loop but never pushes or opens a PR; it prints the diff instead. With no --inference-url, the CLI probes local endpoints and logs using inference endpoint … (auto-discovered). Every run_shell and browser_* call stops at a [y/N] prompt. See Coding Sessions.
data.run-the-apps-locally#Run the apps locall:
core dev up runs the apps natively (no VMs, no images, no sudo in the run loop): both app backends, the shared inference server (mistralrs-server), the Flutter UIs, and the security stack (envelope encryption, pipe mesh, rotating raft mTLS, eBPF).
core dev up # everything (the default is all) core dev up face # one app core dev down # stop everything Things core dev up needs:
The app checkouts. It reads the environment variables FACE_REPO and PULSE_REPO (defaults ../face and ../pulse), not the CLI’s --face-repo flag. A mistralrs-server binary and GGUF weights. Without them it logs mistralrs-server binary or model not found under … — apps spawn their own if configured. and carries on. Flutter, for the console UI. Without it you see console skipped (flutter not found). Run state goes under .dev/: logs are .dev/*-{backend,frontend}.log, PIDs are .dev/.pid, and ports are written to .dev/ports.env. On first run it mints a dev mesh CA and generates a per-machine envelope KEK at .dev/secrets/CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK with crypto/rand (delete that file to rotate it).
data.sign-in-to-github#Sign in to GitHub: core auth login # GitHub Device Flow, cached in ~/.core/auth.json core auth status core session uses this token by default. It switches to GitHub App installation tokens only when CORE_GH_APP_ID and CORE_GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY (or CORE_GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE) are set, which is meant for unattended runs.
