data.onboarding-settings#Onboarding (Settings:
The workspace records which sources and agents Atlas may use and which data-quality (DQ) engine runs. WorkspaceService.GetWorkspace computes the onboarding checklist against what exists now. A granted source that has since been deleted from the registry shows as missing, not as granted.
Step key Label Required discover_agents Discover agents No grant_sources Grant app access Yes select_engine Connect DQ engine Yes confirm Confirm Yes CompleteOnboarding fails with FAILED_PRECONDITION and lists every unmet step unless both of these hold:
at least one granted source exists in TIDE’s connection registry, and a connectable DQ engine is selected. The error reads onboarding cannot be completed; unmet: ….
Only TIDE’s own engine, core-capex, is connectable. ListDqEngines also lists Atlas’s four third-party engines as NOT_CONNECTABLE, with the reason and with absent rule counts.
Granting a source never dials it. UpdateWorkspace checks that each source_ids entry exists in TIDE’s registry, and that each agent_ids entry is a registered agent. It records permission and nothing more.
A registered agent is metadata only. TIDE never calls, polls, authenticates to or sends data to an agent in the enterprise agent registry. The contract has no endpoint, token or credential field. last_seen is always absent, with a reason.
ResetWorkspace (note required) clears only the workspace settings and re-opens onboarding. CapEx feeds, scan history, rule governance, decisions and the agent registry are untouched.
data.the-rail-in-order#The rail, in order: Page (rail label) ?tab= What it reads Overview dqOverview Tabs: DQ overview: /api/data-governance-findings, /api/rules-recon, /api/compliance, /api/connections, /api/governance-runs, Resolve ListSources / GetSourceDescription, CapexService.GetAnalystDashboard for the CapEx DQ score; Capital Governance Analyst (?tab=analystDashboard, ?tab=dashboards): CapexService.GetAnalystDashboard, /api/measures, /api/governance-runs, /api/data-governance-findings; CFO Cockpit (?tab=cfoDashboard): CapexService.GetCfoDashboard, /api/finops (every $ is a showback estimate: allocated computeUnits × the $0.10 per 100 CU rate, never a charge), /api/compliance; History (?tab=progress): CapexService.ListScanRuns, /api/maturity, /api/governance-runs, the governance findings history. The header gear opens Settings (?tab=settings): WorkspaceService GetWorkspace, ListDqEngines, the onboarding wizard, ResetWorkspace; read-only /api/rules-recon, /api/github. While onboarding is not complete, a Set up Intelligence call to action opens the same panel Estate resolve Tabs: Resolve: the shared estate component (runink.ui.estate.v1.EstateService) — each Test / Explore / Access patterns / Map estate confirm asks where it runs (the source’s own runner, Runink managed, or a self-hosted runner from /api/runners); see Resolve; Lineage (?tab=lineage): /api/data-lineage plus datagov fail/warn hotspots, and the “Declared derivations” a Resolve Explore recorded CapEx capexMonitor Tabs: Capex Monitor: CapexService GetSummary, GetFeeds, GetConfig, ListFindings, GetRuleBook; writes StageFeed → PreviewIngest → CommitIngest (or PullFeed, which asks where the pull runs), ClearFeed, UpdateConfig; Capex Lineage (?tab=capexLineage): ListFindings, TraceFinding, GetRuleBook; Remediation (?tab=remediation): GovernanceService ListRemediations, DryRunRemediation, DecideRemediation, ListDecisions, a link to Trust › Harness for the platform findings, then /api/compliance per control and sign-off & audit (/api/agents, /api/governance) Business Rules rules GovernanceService ListRules, ListRuleChanges. Writes: ProposeRuleChange, DecideRuleChange, SetRuleOwner. Below that, the shared rules-reconciliation view: RulesReconService.GetRulesRecon Playbooks orchestrator PlaybookService (list, get, events, dispatchable agents, and the writes). The cron schedules outside any playbook are on DevEx › Agent runs › Schedules & arming, linked from here The Data audit is the third tile of the Overview’s verdict strip (?tab=dataAudit opens its panel). See Data audit & lineage. Instances by initiative are DevEx › Cluster › Instances’ Group by initiative (?tab=pmoDashboard lands there).
data.where-the-pages-come-from#Where the page:
Intelligence follows the partner product Atlas page for page: layout, sections and copy. Each view draws an AtlasSourceRef chip, so you can hover to see the source of every screen.
The data is TIDE’s, never Atlas’s. Every figure comes from a TIDE endpoint. If TIDE has no source for a section, the section keeps its Atlas layout and draws an absent panel with the reason.
Two things differ from Atlas:
Resolve is not an Atlas page. It is ported from FACE’s Reconcile and Data Connectors pages, and it shows a FaceSourceRef chip instead of an AtlasSourceRef chip. Agents is DataEx › Agents (see DataEx). ?tab=agents still lands on it.
data.who-may-do-what#Who may do what: Reads need only a console session. Every write passes the per-method policy table, atlasPolicies. Most writes need an Atlas admin. The allowlist env var for that is CORE_ATLAS_ADMINS. When it is unset, every identity the console admits counts as an Atlas admin. See Rule governance for the four classes.

data:
Business Rules and Remediation read the console’s Atlas governance API, GovernanceService (runink.core.atlas.v1).
In Runink TIDE a rule’s status, owner and Approve / Edit actions each change what is scored.
data.policy-classes-atlaspolicies#Policy clas:
Every Atlas RPC has exactly one class in atlasPolicies. A method missing from the table is treated as admin-write, so it fails closed.
Class Who may call Examples read Any admitted identity, including on an open console ListRules, ListRemediations, DryRunRemediation, ListDecisions attributable-write A session on a console with sign-in configured ProposeRuleChange decider-write Attributable at the gate. The handler then requires the rule owner or an Atlas admin, never the proposer, inside the governance store’s CAS DecideRuleChange, DecideRemediation, ActivatePlaybook, DecideApproval admin-write adminRefusal with CORE_ATLAS_ADMINS SetRuleOwner, every CapEx write, every workspace write CORE_ATLAS_ADMINS is optional. Unset means every identity this console admits (sign-in itself fails closed through CONSOLE_ALLOWED_EMAILS / _HD). Set, it narrows admin rights to the list.
On a console with no sign-in, reads are allowed and every other class is refused. Every non-read attempt is audited under resource atlas-governance, with actions such as atlas.rules.propose, atlas.rules.decide, atlas.remediation.decide and atlas.rules.owner. That includes refusals at the gate and four-eyes denials by the handler.
data.proposing-and-deciding-changes-four-eyes:
A rule change is proposed by one identity and decided by another.
RuleChangeKind Carries STATUS rule_id + proposed_status PARAMETER parameter (and optionally rule_id) NEW_RULE new_rule (title, expression, sheet, severity) A rationale is required for every proposal (rationale is required — a change nobody can explain is not reviewable).
PARAMETER changes may set only the engine thresholds in govParamDefs. The allowed ranges exclude values that would switch a rule off by arithmetic. A rule is switched off by a REJECTED status, visibly.
Parameter Tunes Range tolerance_days how far dates may drift from the plan 0..365, whole days unit_price_capital_threshold the unit price that separates capital from non-capital items 0.01..1e9 approval_lag_min_days the minimum time between a request and its approval 0..365, whole days request_plan_tolerance_pct how far a request may differ from its plan line 0..100 overspend_factor how far spend may exceed its approval before it needs more 1..10 DecideRuleChange approves or rejects an OPEN change. The decider must be the rule’s owner or an Atlas admin, and never the proposer. A proposer who tries to decide gets:
four eyes: … proposed … and may not decide it — it needs … (the proposer may only WITHDRAW)
The proposer may withdraw their own open change (DECISION_WITHDRAW), and that is the only decision they may make. Approving applies the change:
a status change re-scopes scoring; a threshold change updates the engine configuration; a new rule is recorded as approved but unevaluated. A rule may have only one open change at a time (… already has an open change (…) — decide or withdraw it first).
A NEW rule is never evaluated. TIDE has no evaluator for free-text expressions, and pretending to run one would fabricate a verdict. The rule is stored and governed, and its effect stays RULE_EFFECT_NOT_EVALUATED. SetRuleOwner names (or clears) the identity that decides a rule’s changes and remediations. It is admin only. The owner must be an email address as the console knows it.
data.rules-reconciliation-the-recon-agent#Rul:
Below the governance section, Business Rules shows /api/rules-recon: the recon agent’s reconciliation of the tenant’s governance rule book against the CapEx engine the console runs. Each rule gets one verdict:
Verdict Meaning Aligned The implementation matches the governing policy Drift The implementation diverges from it (for example an approved threshold differs from the value the engine evaluates with, or a status disagrees with its effect) Shadow Logic exists with no governing policy Missing A policy exists with no implementation (governed but never raised, or a governed id the engine lacks) A fresh workspace is mostly Shadow, and that is correct. The governance document records a rule only when the tenant did something: decided a status change, named an owner, or approved a threshold. A rule running on the engine’s built-in default (approved, no owner) is TIDE’s code, not a policy anyone wrote, so it cites no policy document. Every comparison is deterministic. The model is asked only whether an approved free-text NEW rule is already implemented by an engine rule. Unknown is never a verdict:
an unread governance document is zero rules and complete:false; an engine threshold that could not be read counts as a gap; with no model, new rules are gaps, not Missing. The agent runs daily at 09:37 UTC, on an @core_recon comment, on a manual run, and as a playbook step. It reads its inputs from the console and writes its report back with the token CORE_RECON_INGEST_TOKEN. The browser reads the result through the session-gated GET /api/rules-recon. See the agent fleet.
data.the-decision-log#The decision log: ListDecisions returns rule changes, owner changes, remediation decisions and playbook decisions, newest first. Each DecisionRecord mirrors the audit event that the same write appended to the hash chain, and audit_seq links the two. The governance store keeps a 500-entry decision log.
data.the-remediation-queue#The remediation qu:
ListRemediations returns one item per current finding, scored and dry-run alike, with its fix, the required approver and its state.
FixKind Meaning FIX_KIND_DETERMINISTIC A mechanical rewrite exists (for example, reclassifying an item’s category). DryRunRemediation can simulate it FIX_KIND_ADVISORY The fix needs a human or a source-system action. A dry run answers FAILED_PRECONDITION with the reason (… cannot be dry-run: …), never a simulated guess DryRunRemediation applies a deterministic fix to a copy of the current feeds, re-runs the engine, and returns before/after. It writes nothing, so it is classed as a read. DecideRemediation records APPROVE or DISMISS. It does not modify any feed. TIDE holds a copy of the uploaded feeds, not the source system, and has no write-back path. An approved fix is applied at the source and resolves on the next ingest. A dismissal is bound to the upload of the finding’s sheet, so re-ingesting that sheet re-opens the item if the finding persists. Remediation confidence is always absent. Every fix is the rule book’s remediation, not a model’s inference. (Atlas displayed a hard-coded 89%.)
data.what-a-rule-status-does#What a rule stat: RuleStatus RuleEffect (from the server) Meaning APPROVED RULE_EFFECT_SCORED Findings count in the DQ score, KPIs, dashboards and scan history. The default for every engine rule PENDING, DRAFT RULE_EFFECT_DRY_RUN The rule is still evaluated and its findings are listed with Finding.dry_run, but they are excluded from every figure. Each excluded rule is named in provenance.unmeasured, so a DQ figure never silently changes meaning REJECTED RULE_EFFECT_NOT_EVALUATED The rule is not evaluated, and its findings do not exist Clients read the effect from the server and never derive it from the status. ListRules returns each rule with its status, effect, owner (or the reason there is none), finding count and open changes.

data:
Intelligence › Orchestrator (?tab=orchestrator) is where you manage playbooks. A playbook is a chain of steps with the stage labels detect → validate → remediate → notify → verify. It links a playbook to Runink TIDE’s own agents in both directions:
a playbook step can start an agent; an agent’s report can start a playbook. The contract is PlaybookService (runink.core.atlas.v1).
data.dispatching-agents#Dispatching agents:
Only six agents can be named in dispatch_agent. These are the autonomous ones that need no PR or issue context (pbDispatchable):
datagov · compliance · risk · judge · recon · curator
ListDispatchableAgents returns that set, plus whether the console can dispatch at all right now (a GitHub App is configured and an agents repository is resolved) and why not.
The dispatch goes to /, where CORE_AGENTS_REPO defaults to core. It uses the console’s App installation token. It is a repository_dispatch and not a workflow_dispatch, because the App holds actions: read only.
{ "event_type": "core-playbook", "client_payload": { "agent": "datagov", "playbook_id": "…", "run_id": "…", "step_id": "…", "chain_depth": 0 } } Each of the six agents runs only when the step names it. The payload is validated before the agent sees it: ids must match ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$ and depth must be 0..3.
The job’s last step reports the outcome back. The reported conclusion is the agent step’s outcome, which the job status can make worse but never better. The report is retried on 5xx and network errors. A 4xx is logged and not retried. An undelivered report fails the workflow run, and the console ends that step TIMED_OUT.
A curator dispatched by a playbook is treated exactly like its scheduled run (fleet-wide, with the same dry-run rule), so a playbook can never make it publish more than its cron would. See the agent fleet.
data.events-the-harness-raises#Events the har:
Events fire only after a successful store write, never before. No agent change is needed for any of these.
Agent Event Raised by Attributes datagov findings.reported POST /api/data-governance-findings fail_count, warn_count, and per fail/warn finding control, verdict, domain, connection recon recon.reported POST /api/rules-recon/report drift, shadow, missing, tenant judge judgements.reported POST /api/judgements dissent, unable capex scan.committed a committed CapEx ingest critical, high, medium, findings, dq, rule_id (matches when that rule has at least one scored finding) estate estate.mapped a committed Resolve estate map domains, unplaced, gaps, drift, shadow, missing Any agent may also raise an explicit event through POST /api/playbook-events (below).
data.lifecycle#Lifecycle:
PlaybookStatus How it gets there DRAFT Every playbook is created as a draft. Editing an ACTIVE playbook returns it to DRAFT ACTIVE Only through ActivatePlaybook, by an Atlas admin who neither wrote nor last edited it (four eyes). An active playbook starts agents on its own PAUSED PausePlaybook. ResumePlaybook brings it back Clients may not set status: status is server-managed: a playbook is written as DRAFT and becomes ACTIVE only by ActivatePlaybook (four eyes).
DraftFromFindings builds a DRAFT deterministically from the current CapEx findings (the rules failing most) as capex_scan → approval → notify → capex_scan (verify). No model is involved.
Caps: 100 playbooks, 1..10 steps, 4 triggers per playbook.
data.post-apiplaybook-events#\u003ccode\u003e: {"agent": "datagov", "event": "findings.reported", "subject": "…", "detail": "…", "attributes": {"control": "DG-3", "verdict": "fail"}, "causedByRunId": "…"} It answers 200 {"started": ["PBR-…"], "skipped": [{"playbookId": "…", "reason": "…"}]}. Attributes are string→string, capped at 16 keys of 256 bytes each, and screened like every other free text. They are matched against trigger conditions and never executed. causedByRunId sets the chain depth.
data.post-apiplaybook-runsstep-report#\u003cc: {"runId": "…", "stepId": "…", "agent": "datagov", "conclusion": "success|failure|cancelled|skipped", "detail": "one line", "githubRunUrl": "https://github.com/…/runs/N"} Status Meaning 200 {"accepted": true} 400 Malformed body 401 missing bearer token 403 The token is not the App’s authority for this org 404 Unknown run or step 409 The step is not awaiting a report, or it is another agent’s step The console, not the agent, decides what the conclusion does to the run.
data.runs#Runs:
RunStatus:
Status Meaning RUNNING A step is executing WAITING_AGENT Waiting for a dispatched agent’s step report WAITING_APPROVAL Waiting at a require_approval step SUCCEEDED Every step finished successfully FAILED A step failed REJECTED An approval was rejected CANCELLED CancelRun was called (note required) TIMED_OUT A dispatched agent did not report by the deadline EXPIRED An approval was not decided in time Triggers are MANUAL, SCHEDULE, AGENT_EVENT and CAPEX_EVENT.
The ticker (Start, about every 30 s with jitter) fires cron slots, deadlines and expiries. Each is claimed by CAS, so replicas sharing one appfs root act once.
The whole state is one metadoc, var/lib/atlas-playbooks, with one CAS per state transition. It holds:
100 playbooks; every in-flight run plus the newest 200 finished runs; 300 events. It has a 768 KiB budget. When the budget is reached it first trims history and then refuses.
RunNow starts a run of an ACTIVE playbook by hand. It fails with FAILED_PRECONDITION when the playbook is not ACTIVE or a run is in flight.
data.steps#Steps:
A step has a kind (the Atlas stage label: DETECT, VALIDATE, REMEDIATE, NOTIFY or VERIFY) and exactly one action. The kind is a label for people. The action is what runs.
Action What it does Bounds dispatch_agent Sends repository_dispatch event_type core-playbook to TIDE’s agents repository, then waits for a step report until the deadline. No report by then ends the step TIMED_OUT. A step is never assumed successful agent must be dispatchable. timeout_minutes 5..240, default 60 capex_scan Re-evaluates the current CapEx feeds and records a ScanRun (trigger MANUAL). With compare_to_first_scan, it passes only if the scored finding count (optionally for rule_ids) did not rise compared with the run’s first scan Needs an earlier capex_scan to compare to require_approval Pauses the run until DecideApproval. An empty approver means any Atlas admin, and it is never the run’s initiator. Expiry ends the run EXPIRED. Rejection ends it REJECTED timeout_hours 1..168, default 72 notify Posts one comment of ids and counts on a GitHub issue in the console’s org. It never includes feed rows or finding details. Nothing else is ever contacted repo is a repository name (no owner, no URL). issue is a positive number What no step does: call a model, edit a feed or source system, or contact a registered enterprise agent. expected_lift is always absent, because it would be a forecast TIDE cannot make. success_rate is measured as SUCCEEDED ÷ finished runs, and is absent until a run has finished.
Steps are claimed by CAS before they run and are never re-run. An abandoned claim ends FAILED.
data.the-loop-guard#The loop guard:
An agent that a playbook dispatched will, by doing its job, post the very report that could re-trigger the playbook. So an event is skipped, and the skip is recorded on the event with its reason, when any of these holds:
the playbook is not ACTIVE; a run is already in flight (a run is in flight (…)); the trigger’s cooldown has not passed (cooldown: trigger … started a run at …); the chain depth exceeds 3 (chain depth … exceeds 3 (caused by run …) — refused, not run). ListEvents shows what each event started or skipped, and why.
data.the-two-agent-doors-json#The two agent d: Both doors take the same bearer contract as the agents’ other report ingests: a GitHub App token that carries the App’s authority for the console’s org, verified by authorizeReporter. Bodies are strict, text is screened, and every call is audited.
data.triggers#Triggers: Trigger Fires when manual Only RunNow starts it schedule A 5-field cron in UTC whose minute field is ONE number from 0 to 59, so it fires at most once an hour. Anything else is refused: the minute field must be ONE number 0-59 — a schedule fires at most once an hour agent_event An agent’s event matches every condition (AND). An empty condition list matches every event of that agent and event capex_event The CapEx engine raises scan.committed, the only CapEx event cooldown_minutes sets the minimum time between runs started by the same trigger: 5 to 43,200 (30 days), default 60. A condition is {attribute, op, value}, where op is one of eq, neq, gt, gte or contains. A numeric op on a non-number evaluates to false, never to an error.
data.who-may-do-what#Who may do what: RPC Class Audit action ListPlaybooks, GetPlaybook, ListRuns, GetRun, ListDispatchableAgents, ListEvents read — CreatePlaybook, UpdatePlaybook, DeletePlaybook, DraftFromFindings, PausePlaybook, ResumePlaybook, RunNow, CancelRun admin-write atlas.playbooks.create / .update / .delete / .draft / .pause / .resume / .run / .run.cancel ActivatePlaybook decider-write: an Atlas admin who is not the author or last editor atlas.playbooks.activate DecideApproval decider-write: the named approver or an Atlas admin, never the run’s initiator atlas.playbooks.approval.decide Decisions, dispatches and reports also land in the governance decision log (subject playbook).

Intelligence › Resolve (?tab=resolve) shows what the tenant’s registered sources actually contain:
how their datasets group into data domains; how the sources are used; whether what a source declares about itself agrees with what its data shows. It is ported from FACE’s Reconcile and Data Connectors pages, not from Atlas. It reuses FACE’s estate engine (connect, graph, access).
Resolve is the one place Runink TIDE dials a tenant source. The only other dialer is the admin-only connectorsync probe, POST /api/connectors/status/refresh, which covers the connectors TIDE publishes and never touches registry records. The agents (datagov included), core connection register and granting a source to the workspace all dial nothing.
data.choosing-the-runner#Choosing the runner:
Every action, and CapexService.PullFeed, first decides the effective runner (resEffectiveRunner) from the request’s optional runner field:
runner on the request Effective runner absent (empty) The connection’s binding. An empty binding means console console Runink managed, explicitly, even for a connection bound to a self-hosted runner a runner name That registered runner A name must be a DNS label or console. Anything else gets runner … is not a runner name (a DNS label, or "console" for the Runink managed runner).
console dials in-process. The runner registry is not even read. Actions run on console; a choice of any other runner is refused. No bundle is opened, the engine is not called, and there is no fallback to another runner. The refusal names the state it found:
State found Outcome What the detail says Not registered runner_unknown Enrol that runner, or choose console Revoked runner_revoked Who revoked it and when Pending (not enrolled yet) runner_offline Enrolment is not complete Active, not connected runner_offline TIDE has no live connection to its address Active and connected runner_offline “connected; …”. This never claims the runner is down Registry unreadable failed “runner registry unavailable”. Never runner_unknown In a map run, the runner routes every source, and a refused source becomes a gap in the map. The effective runner, and whether it came from the action or the binding, is recorded in the audit detail and in ActionRecord.runner. Runners themselves are managed on DataEx › Runners.
data.reads-never-dial#Reads never dial:
The read RPCs answer from what the last dialing action committed. Nothing dials on a read, a timer or a page load. A test fails the engine if a read calls it.
The page re-reads GetEstate every 5 seconds only while a map run is RUNNING and the tab is on screen.
data.refusals-you-will-see#Refusals you will: On a console with no sign-in: this console has no sign-in configured, so dialing a tenant source would be unattributable — set GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID or CONSOLE_ADMIN_PASSWORD before testing, exploring or mapping sources. On the page, the first PermissionDenied disables every dial and shows the console’s reason. A FailedPrecondition or InvalidArgument is drawn verbatim and gates nothing else. More in Troubleshooting.
data.storage#Storage:
The documents are metadoc kinds in the console’s appfs root:
Document Contents Budget var/lib/atlas-estate Per-source last action, access counts, map runs 512 KiB var/lib/atlas-estate-map The last committed map 768 KiB var/lib/atlas-estate-desc- One source’s last Explore, with h = sha256(id)[:16] 768 KiB
data.the-four-dialing-actions#The four dialin:
Each is admin-write (CORE_ATLAS_ADMINS). Each is audited under resource atlas-estate with the outcome, including refusals, and each sits behind a confirm dialog on the page that states what it dials and what it keeps.
Action Audit action Budget What it does TestSource atlas.resolve.test 20 s Checks that the source answers with its credentials ExploreSource atlas.resolve.explore 90 s Reads the catalogue: datasets, columns, types, declared keys, view dependencies, and profile statistics where the engine has them ReadAccessPatterns atlas.resolve.access 90 s Reads the source’s own access views over a window of window_days 1..90 MapEstate atlas.resolve.map 15 min per run, 30 s per source Builds the estate domain map across sources. It returns at once and runs in the background, one run in flight per console A second map while one is running is refused: map run … started by … at … is still in flight; one run at a time.
Credentials are opened with the registry’s audited Credentials read for one engine call and then dropped. They are never stored, returned on the wire, logged or handed to an agent. Engine errors are scrubbed (resScrub) before they are recorded.
data.the-values-boundary#The values boundary:
The estate adapter is the boundary where values stop. It copies structure and counts field by field into record types that have no field for a cell, MIN/MAX, a sample row, a principal name or a credential. Tests guard this boundary.
Kept Never kept Datasets, columns, types, nullability, declared keys Sampled values, sample rows Row counts, NULL counts, DISTINCT counts (with their basis) MIN / MAX / mean (a customer cell) Access counts: reads, writes, distinct principals Principal names Outcome, time and actor of each action Credentials Explore profiling limits. Where the engine supports statistics, Explore computes per-column aggregates over at most 25 datasets (resMaxStatDatasets). Only DISTINCT and NULL counts cross the boundary. Explore also keeps the statistics pass’s counted row count.
No confidence number. Domains carry an evidence class (declared, measured or weak) and every edge carries an evidence kind. A GUESS edge is drawn dotted in the warning tone and is never styled like a declared key.
data.two-services-one-set-of-documents#Two se:
The page is the shared estate component (runink.ui.estate.v1.EstateService).
The older runink.core.atlas.v1.ResolveService stays registered as a deprecated alias for one release. The CapEx pull dialog, the connection wizard’s “Test after saving” and the audit pages still call it. Both services read and write the same three stored documents, so each sees the other’s writes.
EstateService ResolveService (deprecated) Class ListSources, GetSourceDescription, GetAccessPatterns, GetEstateMap, GetReconciliation ListSources, GetSourceDescription, GetAccessPatterns, GetEstate, GetReconciliation read TestSource, ExploreSource, ReadAccessPatterns, MapEstate the same four admin-write
data.what-resolve-records-as-data-lineage#Wha:
When an Explore, ReadAccessPatterns or MapEstate commits, the console records what it observed as data lineage. This happens in process: there is no HTTP hop and no ingest token. The edges go into the same observed-lineage store the apps publish into, under the publisher core-resolve. The app ingest refuses that publisher name from anyone else with a 403.
Edge kind Between From DECLARED_FOREIGN_KEY dataset → dataset Explore’s declared keys, and the map’s declared keys INFERRED_* placement dataset → domain The map, only for domains whose members come from two or more sources OBSERVED_ACCESS dataset → principals Access counts, only where a stated read or write count is above zero DECLARED_VIEW_DEPENDENCY base → view The source’s own catalogue: Postgres pg_depend, MySQL VIEW_TABLE_USAGE. The Lineage page draws these as “Declared derivations” Not recorded: GUESSED_COLUMN_OVERLAP (a guess is not an observation) and catalogue containment.
Each edge carries only qualified names, the kind, counts and provenance. It carries no constraint or column name, no detail text and no admin identity.
Edges are deduplicated source→destination. Each commit replaces its own scope’s claims (explore:, access:, map), and claims expire after 30 days. The Resolve lineage key is capped at 256 edges / 512 KiB, and the weakest edges are dropped first and counted.
A committed map also raises the playbook harness event estate / estate.mapped, with attributes domains, unplaced, gaps, drift, shadow and missing. See Playbooks.

data:
A model card says, in plain words, what one of Runink TIDE’s agents does, what it reads, what it produces, what a person still decides, which model it runs on, and its scope. There is one card for each agent you meet in the console, in a pull request or in an issue. Agents that work as a pair share a card.
Every card has the same eight parts: what it does, what it reads, what it produces, human oversight, model, where it runs and data handling, guardrails, and scope.
data.not-given-a-card#Not given a card: eval is a test harness for the agents themselves, not an agent you meet. Its trace-scoring step uses the general model. users applies access grants from an add-users issue. It uses no model. session is the core session coding agent, which you drive yourself. See Coding Sessions. The Fix Drafter’s resolver and FORGE’s forger use it.
data.the-base-models#The base models: Tier Model Maker Licence Used by coder Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B Qwen Apache-2.0 Code Reviewer, Fix Drafter, CI Doctor (failed-build diagnosis), the FORGE coding step general Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Qwen Apache-2.0 every other agent that calls a model The Independent Assessor also uses a small ranking model, Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (Qwen, Apache-2.0), to narrow evidence. The Data Governance Checker uses no model at all.
data.the-cards#The cards: Card Agent Model What a person decides Code Reviewer reviewer coder which findings matter and what merges Fix Drafter fixer, resolver coder whether to merge the draft correction CI Doctor self-heal, opsdoctor coder (self-heal), general (opsdoctor) whether to apply the proposed fix Issue Triager triage general the final labels and who works on the issue Backlog Hunter hunter general what to do about each reported item Dependency Risk risk general which upgrades to schedule Compliance Evidence compliance general how to close a gap; any claim of compliance Release Curator curator general whether to merge the curator’s pull request Independent Assessor judge general, with a ranking model what to do with each verdict Rules Reconciler recon general, for one question whether to fix the rule or the engine Data Governance Checker datagov no model owners, credentials and masking Task Deployer deployer general whether to merge the release-notes pull request Ask TIDE console Ask and chat general what to do with an answer; every provisioning action FORGE FORGE planner, forger general (planner), coder (code) every planned step, and every merge The roster names in the second column are the ones the Agent Fleet page uses.
data.three-things-true-of-every-card#Three th: Agents propose; people decide. No TIDE agent merges a pull request, deploys a change or sends anything outside your organisation by itself. Your own inference. Every agent calls the model plane of your own TIDE deployment, on your Server or in your cloud. No third-party AI service is called. See Models & inference. Open base models. Agents run on open base models, listed below.

data: The console’s question service, and its provisioning chat. See also Ask.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Figures are checked by the server: a number that is not verbatim in a tool result is removed from the answer. It is instructed never to produce confidence scores, quality ratings or personal-data judgements of its own. Tool results are untrusted data, and the model is told to ignore instructions inside them. Questions and answers are screened by the guardrails. Its tools only read; a chat action changes nothing until a person confirms it. An Ask question has a length limit, and each run a step and time budget.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person decides what to do with an answer. Every state-changing chat action needs a person’s confirmation before it runs. Ask acts for the signed-in person, and refuses on a console with no sign-in.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented records. “Why is project P-114 flagged?” Ask TIDE looks up the project’s findings, then traces one. Answer: “P-114 has 3 open findings. F-2231 (unit price above threshold) traces to purchase order PO-77812, line 4, unit price 812.00.” Every figure in the answer came from a tool result.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
data.scope#Scope: It reports the figures the systems hold, as they hold them: it quotes them rather than summing or converting them. Delivery (DevEx) questions are outside its scope. When inference is not configured, it says so and calls no model.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
You ask a question in plain words. Runink TIDE looks it up with its own tools and answers only with figures it can point to.
Intelligence questions: CapEx findings and their traces, the rule book, remediations, playbook runs, lineage, the systems inventory and data-governance findings. DataEx questions: model cards, the agent roster, autonomy settings, the harness findings queue, judgements and inference status. Provisioning chat: from a sentence, it proposes one action, such as listing instances or creating an instance for an app and tenant.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A streamed answer in which every figure appears verbatim in a tool result, cited to a record that holds that value. A clear “could not look” with the reason, when a source cannot be read, rather than “nothing found”. For the chat: one proposed action, waiting for confirmation.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Only what TIDE already holds, through read tools, one per step. Each question is scoped to Intelligence or DataEx, and the tools available depend on that scope.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Questions and tool results go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. When the deployment’s console is set up to sign its model requests, a person’s question is queued ahead of background agent work.

data: Roster name: hunter.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: The model only sorts comment text into vulnerability mention, follow-up promise or neither. Every other decision is a fact read from the Git host. It never closes a security issue without a merged fix. It never merges or closes a pull request; on a pull request it only removes a stale review:findings-open label. A “Duplicate of” note counts only from someone who could close the issue themselves. Comments are marked as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised, and screened before the model reads them. A small cap on writes per run. Comments it could not classify are reported as unclassified, never hidden.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person decides what to act on. The hunter stays dry until an administrator arms it. Once armed it closes an issue only when a merged pull request closes it, or when an owner, member or collaborator of the repository marked it a duplicate of an issue closed as completed. It may also remove a stale review:findings-open label once a later clean review supersedes it. Everything it cannot prove is reported as needing a person.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented comment. On a closed pull request a reviewer wrote: “this export endpoint skips the permission check for service accounts, we should revisit.” No later merged change touches it. The report lists it as an unresolved vulnerability mention with a link to the comment.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
data.scope#Scope: Each run covers the pull requests closed since its previous run. It reads the conversation held on the Git host. It reports; a person decides the fix.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It rereads the review conversations on recently closed pull requests and reports the security concerns nobody resolved and the follow-ups nobody picked up.
Finds vulnerability mentions with no later fix, and promised follow-ups with no issue or pull request that tracks them. Flags lingering work: old open issues and pull requests, work carried across several milestones, and stale review:findings-open labels. It also flags pull requests merged while findings were still open. Closes an issue only when it can prove the work is done.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: One run report per run, shown in the console. Once armed, a living “Backlog hunter report” issue with a section per repository. A dry run reports to the console only. An evidence comment before any issue it closes.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Every comment, review and reviewer finding on the pull requests closed since its last run, in every repository Runink TIDE can reach. The open issues and pull requests, and facts from your Git host such as links, dates and merged commits.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Review comments go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.

data: Roster names: self-heal and opsdoctor. See also the Agent Fleet.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: One comment per failure, checked first: a wrong root cause sends the author the wrong way, so a dissent withholds it. Logs are evidence, never instructions. A failing test can print anything, so log text is marked as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised. Opsdoctor is asked to name the log or state it would need when the evidence is thin, instead of guessing. Bounded repair: the doctor’s repairs are capped per run and confined to the build plane. The exact rules it acts on are not published.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person applies any code fix. Self-heal never pushes code. Opsdoctor makes only small, bounded repairs to the build plane itself. Anything bigger goes to a person.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented failure. A test fails with want "degraded", got "healthy". Self-heal comments: “Root cause: the new order checks readiness before restarts, so a crash-looping pod reads as healthy. Fix: move the restart check first (diff attached).” The author applies it.
data.model#Model: Self-heal: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier). Opsdoctor: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
data.scope#Scope: Self-heal works on a job that ran and failed. Jobs that never started are opsdoctor’s. It diagnoses the build. Application code and delivery metrics are outside its scope. A job stopped by the Git host’s own account limits is not diagnosed.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
When a build fails, it posts one root-cause comment with a proposed fix. When the build machines themselves stop working, it reports why and makes one bounded repair.
Self-heal: diagnoses a CI run that ran and failed. Opsdoctor: checks the self-hosted build plane every 30 minutes for runners and jobs that are stuck or failing.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Self-heal: one comment that cites the job and the log lines, names the root cause and gives a short proposed diff. It goes on the pull request when the run has one, and otherwise on a tracking issue for that workflow. If the independent check dissents, a “withheld” notice posts instead. If it could not decide, the comment says NOT VERIFIED. Opsdoctor: one comment on a tracking issue with the most likely cause and the next action, and the crash evidence it read, including log tails. A “did not diagnose” notice, rather than a silent pass, when the model cannot be reached or returns nothing usable.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Self-heal: the names of the failing jobs and the tail of each job’s log. Opsdoctor: the state of the runner pods and the CI job queue, and the last log lines of a crashing pod in the namespaces it watches (the build plane and the platform’s own services). It reads no CI job logs.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Build logs go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Opsdoctor runs outside CI on purpose, so it can still report when CI is down, and it calls the inference engine directly.

data: Roster name: reviewer. See also the Review Pipeline.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: It is instructed to report only concrete, checkable findings that name the defect and where it is, and never to claim that code is unused or undefined, because the caller may sit outside the diff. A finding outside the fixed severity levels or without a plausible file path is dropped, and the review says how many were dropped. The diff is evidence, not instructions. It is marked as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised, and instructions written into the code are reviewed as text. The reviewer can only comment: it has no way to approve or merge. The incoming diff and the outgoing review are both screened before the review posts.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person reads the findings and decides what merges. The reviewer cannot approve, merge or push.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented change. A pull request adds an early return err inside a function that holds a lock. The review lists: 🟠 retry/backoff.go:47 — the new return leaves mu locked; add defer mu.Unlock() after the Lock. The Fix Drafter then drafts a correction for the author to accept or close.
data.model#Model: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier).
data.scope#Scope: It reviews the change, not the whole codebase. It reviews what it is shown, without running the code or its tests. A diff larger than the review window is read from the start, and the review says how much was read and that the rest is unreviewed.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It reviews every pull request the same way, line by line, and names each defect it finds with the file, the line and the fix.
Reviews a pull request when it opens or changes, or when someone asks with a review tag such as @core_review. Reviews pull requests in repositories that have no review set up of their own, through the central sweep. Hands every finding to the Fix Drafter.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: One pull request review that lists every finding: severity, file, line, the defect, and the fix. A finding with a file and line is also attached to that line. The review:findings-open label when findings remain. Only a completed review with no findings clears it. A “did not run” notice, rather than a silent pass, whenever no review was made: the model could not be reached, the diff could not be read, the answer was not in the review format, or the review could not be posted. The check then closes as neutral, not as passed.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The pull request’s unified diff: the added lines and their context. Nothing outside the diff. It does not read the rest of the repository.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The diff goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Findings are posted to the pull request on your Git host.

data: Roster name: compliance.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Evidence, never a verdict: it is instructed not to give one, and certification and compliance-status claims in its answer are removed and counted before anything is filed. Unseen is not missing: evidence in a repository it cannot read is UNVERIFIED, never drift and never satisfied. Cited source code is passed in as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised, not as instructions. Its answer cannot carry hidden markers or tags into the report.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person fixes a gap or updates the index, and files the evidence. Any statement that you are compliant comes from a person and an external auditor, never from this agent. Its workflow can read the repository but not change it.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented control. “All service-to-service traffic uses mutual TLS” cites two files, and both still exist. The evidence record: “The server’s TLS settings require and verify client certificates and set TLS 1.3 as the minimum. Suggestion: certificate lifetime is fixed in code; move it to configuration so the evidence can cite one value.”
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
data.scope#Scope: It checks the controls in the index. A citation shows where a control is evidenced, not that it works; each night the close reads examine a few controls in depth. Vulnerable dependencies are Dependency Risk’s job, and auditing each change is Release Curator’s.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
It records evidence for the controls you claim, and flags controls whose cited implementation has gone. It never declares you compliant.
Checks every control in the platform’s control index against the files, folders or workflows it cites. Reads a few controls closely each night and writes down the evidence an auditor will ask for. Supplies a customer-safe evidence block for the release notes.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: The living “Compliance status” issue: a posture per framework and every control whose citation no longer exists, listed as drift. Evidence it cannot see, listed as UNVERIFIED rather than missing. An evidence record per closely read control: what the code does, where, and any suggested improvement. A control-evidence artifact for the audit pack.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The control index: the controls, the framework clauses each maps to (PCI-DSS, SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO 31000, ISO/IEC 42001), and what each cites. For the close reads, the source code each control cites.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Source code goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.

data: Roster name: datagov. See also Data governance.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: No model and no values: findings are rule outputs over structure and counts. Unassessable is never a pass. A verdict per control, per source, rather than a blended score.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person assigns owners, rotates credentials and adds masks. The checker changes nothing.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented connection. A Postgres connection declares no owner and keeps a credential in its address, and Explore recorded a personal-data column without masking. Findings: ownership fail, credential in address fail, personal-data exposure warn, each with the column path or setting name involved. Transport uses TLS: pass.
data.model#Model: None. Every finding is computed by rules. This agent calls no model.
data.scope#Scope: A source is assessed once it has been explored. Its personal-data findings are a starting point for review, not a guarantee that every sensitive column was found. It reflects the structure as of the last Explore.
data.what-it-does#What it does: Every day it checks each connected data source for an owner, safe credentials, encrypted transport, data quality and personal-data exposure, without reading a single row.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
Per connection, a result for each control: pass, warn, fail, or unable to assess (with the reason). The controls cover ownership, credential handling, transport, structural data quality, and personal-data exposure; see Data governance. What each control looks for is deliberately not published.
The findings go to the living “Data governance status” issue and the console’s findings store. A source nobody explored is reported unassessable, with the reason.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The tenant’s connection registry. The structure and counts that Resolve’s Explore recorded: tables, columns, types, null counts and keys. Never values.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment. It holds no credential and dials no data source: it reads only what Explore already recorded. No row or cell value is read.

data: Roster name: risk.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: It is instructed never to invent an advisory, and the scanner’s raw findings are attached to every report, so each advisory the summary names can be checked against them. Reachable advisories are listed first, by the scanner’s reachability. A clear split of duties: your own code changes are the Release Curator’s security audit; controls are Compliance Evidence’s.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person schedules the upgrades. The agent changes nothing itself.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented scan. Seven advisories across four modules: one reachable, four not called, one with no fix, one toolchain. Posture: “1 reachable advisory needs an upgrade today.” The no-fix module gets a recommendation to replace it with a library the platform already uses.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
data.scope#Scope: It covers Go dependencies, as the scanner sees them. It reports the advisories published in the vulnerability database. First-party code is reviewed by the Code Reviewer.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Every day it writes one ranked report on which known vulnerabilities in your Go dependencies your code actually reaches, and what to do about each.
Puts reachable advisories first. Recommends an upgrade, a pin, a patch or a replacement for each advisory. Names the Go version to move to for toolchain advisories.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: The living “Dependency risk report” issue: a one-line posture, the reachable advisories with module and fixed version, a recommendation for each advisory with no upstream fix, and the toolchain advice. When the scan is empty, it says exactly that.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The machine output of Go’s call-graph-aware vulnerability scanner (govulncheck), run by core scan --json across the platform’s modules. Reachability comes from the scanner, not from the model.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The scan output goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. The scanner itself reads the public Go vulnerability database.

data: Roster names: fixer and resolver. See also the Review Pipeline.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Minimal by instruction: it changes only what the findings require. A patch may touch only files the pull request already changes, and never the files that decide how code is built, checked or fetched; those stay with people. Checked before it acts: the Independent Assessor’s plan check judges each patch against the findings and the diff. A dissent means nothing is pushed. Text in the diff that asks for changes is treated as data, not as a request. The patch’s added lines are screened before it is pushed.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person reviews the draft and decides whether to merge it. Merging re-runs the review, so a finding counts as resolved only when the reviewer agrees. The Fix Drafter never merges.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented finding. high, client/put.go, 88: the response body is never closed. The fixer reads the file and drafts one added line, defer resp.Body.Close(). The plan check concurs, TIDE opens the draft pull request, and the developer merges it.
data.model#Model: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier). The plan check before it pushes runs on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0.
data.scope#Scope: It works from review findings. CI and build configuration stay with people. After its retries, an unresolved finding stays open for a person.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
When the Code Reviewer finds a defect, it drafts the smallest correction as a draft pull request and leaves the merge to a person.
Fixer: a one-shot patch for every review finding, of any severity. Resolver: when the fixer cannot fix it, a multi-step coding session on the branch that reads, edits and builds, then opens a further draft. It retries with a larger budget before handing back to people. Can also be asked by hand with an @core_fix comment on the pull request.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A draft pull request onto the reviewed branch, carrying a minimal unified diff. When it does not produce a patch (it answers “no change”, the patch does not apply, or the plan check dissents), a comment on the pull request saying the findings are unresolved; from the automatic review path they then go to the resolver. A draft titled [not verified by the judge] when the independent check could not decide or was switched off.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The pull request’s diff and the reviewer’s findings. The current content of the first files the pull request changes, within a size budget. The repository’s agent instructions file, when it has one. For the resolver: the files of the branch it works on.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The code goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. The resolver’s builds run on your own CI runners.

data:
The FORGE planner, and the forger that builds what it plans. See also FORGE.
The forger is disarmed by default.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Nothing is filed or built until a person approves. The canvas offers only components from the approved catalogue and the connections the project may use. The planner’s steps are checked by the shared judgement checks before they are offered, and the planner’s own verdict words are removed. Settings whose names look like credentials are refused. The coding step is instructed not to call an external AI service, deploy or merge, or change databases or CI, and its pull request is a draft a person reviews.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person approves or edits every proposed step, and a brief is filed only after approval, word for word. A person reviews and merges the forger’s pull request. FORGE never merges or deploys.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented project. “Add a pipeline that collects reefer temperatures from the yard’s MQTT broker into a table, with lineage.” FORGE proposes one new pipeline with a brief; the owner places it as a lane on an approved connection, with three catalogue components, and approves with one edit, “keep 90 days”. The brief is filed, and the forger later opens a draft pull request with the pipeline for the owner to review.
data.model#Model: Planner: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier). Forger’s coding step: Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier).
data.scope#Scope: The canvas works from the approved catalogue; anything else needs a person. It does not deploy, merge, or touch CI or databases.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Describe the application or data pipeline you want. FORGE proposes the work, you shape it as lanes on a canvas, nothing is filed until you approve, and then Runink TIDE drafts the code as a pull request.
Planner (FORGE chat): proposes steps, each a new app or a change to an existing one, with a brief for each. You edit the lanes and components on the canvas yourself. Forger: once armed, takes the oldest open brief that FORGE filed after your approval and that nobody has edited since, and drafts the code as a draft pull request. Any other brief is left for a person, and the run says which.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: Planner: a reply and a list of proposed steps, shown on the canvas for approval. Forger: a draft pull request with the pipeline or app code. TIDE checks that it builds; it does not run tests. Every forged commit is then checked by TIDE’s central verification.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: Planner: your message, the apps that already exist, and the app you selected. Forger: the filed brief and the project’s repository.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Briefs and code go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. FORGE is served inside the TIDE console, on your TIDE sign-in.

data: Roster name: judge. See also Judgements.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Arithmetic before language: a measured claim is recomputed from the evidence’s own numbers, and a mismatch is a dissent. Deterministic checks run before any model call. Never agreement by default: missing, unreadable, off-subject or stale evidence, or an unreachable model, produces unable to judge with the reason. Verdicts are never averaged into a score or an agreement rate. Evidence is marked as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised, and screened by the guardrails; flagged or unassessable evidence is unable to judge, never a verdict.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person decides what to do with each verdict. A verdict does not change the finding’s owner system, and TIDE does not call the external platform back.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented figures. A platform claims “the null rate of customer_id is at most 2%” with evidence of 310 nulls in 10,000 rows. TIDE recomputes 3.1% from those two counts and answers dissent: “The evidence shows a null rate of 3.1%, above the 2% claimed.” A second claim arrives with no evidence: unable to judge, “no evidence was submitted.”
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier), for the qualitative remainder. Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0, to narrow long evidence before the language model sees it. A small decision-tree model answers only the clear cases at the model step; anything it does not answer goes to the language model.
data.scope#Scope: It judges the evidence submitted, without fetching more. Subjects TIDE has no standing over are marked out of scope by the console, not judged. The docket fills once a submitting platform is configured; see Judgements.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Before you act on a finding from another assessment platform, it reads the evidence itself and says whether it agrees, disagrees, or could not judge.
Judges findings that an external platform submitted to Runink TIDE. Runs the same checks as a plan check on the Fix Drafter’s patches, CI Doctor’s diagnoses and Issue Triager’s labels before any of them acts.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: One verdict per finding, with a reason: concur, dissent or unable to judge. Separately, the console marks a finding about a subject TIDE has no standing over as out of scope. Verdicts appear on the DataEx › Judgements page and in the living “Judgement status” issue. Each model-based verdict records which path produced it.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: For each finding: the claim, and the evidence it relied on, such as excerpts, records and measured values. The model is never told the submitter’s own stance.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Findings and evidence go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Findings arrive through TIDE’s own intake.

data: Roster name: triage.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Fixed vocabulary: a label outside the allowed list is discarded, and category and priority must be one of the fixed values. Checked before it acts: the Independent Assessor’s plan check judges the label set first. Instructions inside the issue are treated as text: an issue cannot set its own priority. The issue is screened before it is classified.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: Applying labels is a deliberate exception to “a person approves every change”: the triager applies its labels itself, without waiting for a person. It may do so because the labels come only from a fixed allowed list that contains no label which starts an agent, a workflow or a merge; because the labels are withheld when the independent check dissents or the issue is flagged for review; and because the comment says what was applied and anyone with triage rights can change it. A person decides everything else: who works on the issue, and whether it is closed or solved. The triager does not assign, close or solve anything.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented issue. “The console shows ‘Cannot reach the console API’ after an upgrade; the runners page is blank.” Triage comment: category bug, priority high, labels bug, runners; missing: the console’s log from the upgrade window and the previous version.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
data.scope#Scope: It classifies; investigating and reproducing stay with people. It reads the issue as opened. When the model cannot be reached, it posts a degraded notice rather than labels.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Each new issue gets a one-line summary, a category, a priority and labels, and the labels go on only when an independent check agrees.
Classifies a new issue as bug, feature, question, docs, security or chore. Sets a priority. It is instructed to reserve critical for security problems and data loss. Notes what information is missing.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A triage comment: summary, category, priority, and what is missing. Up to four labels, chosen only from the repository’s allowed list. The comment with the labels withheld, when the independent check dissents or the issue is flagged for human review. NOT VERIFIED when the check could not decide.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The new issue’s title and body.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The issue text goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.

data: Roster name: curator.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Grounded or dropped: a second pass scores every draft against the raw diff. A draft that is not judged grounded, or scores below the threshold, is dropped whole; nothing is published from it. Screened before it is public: everything it publishes (release notes, the documentation report and audits in its pull request, comments on issues and pull requests) is checked by the output guardrails first. A flagged item is not posted, and the run’s log names the rule. It is instructed never to invent files, APIs or vulnerabilities, and the grounding pass is the check on that instruction. A “Satisfied” in the change audit is a reading of one change, not a certification.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person reviews and merges the curator’s pull request. It never merges its own work. A scheduled run stays dry, publishing, commenting and deleting nothing, until an administrator turns that off. A dry run does not count as curated: the next armed run covers the same changes.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented changes. Nine pull requests merged. The draft release notes have seven bullets. The grounding pass finds that “adds single sign-on” has no supporting change (the diff only renames a field) and judges the draft not grounded, so the release notes are left out of this run’s pull request and the run’s log says why.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
data.scope#Scope: It works from what merged, without testing the code. Known vulnerabilities in dependencies are Dependency Risk’s job. A green dry run published nothing.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Every day it reads what merged since its last run and drafts the release notes, a documentation report, an audit of those changes and test scenarios, then drops any draft the changes do not support.
Release notes: an Added / Changed / Fixed section. Stale documentation: the sections a change made wrong or incomplete, with what to change and why. Change security audit: security issues the change introduces, with severity, CWE/OWASP mapping and a fix. Change compliance audit: control-relevant changes mapped to SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 42001 criteria, each marked Satisfied, Gap or Needs-evidence. Thread replies and test scenarios: a short status note on related issues, and a short checklist of user-test scenarios.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A pull request carrying the release notes, the documentation report and the two audits, plus short comments on open issues and pull requests that your organisation’s own members opened. Test scenarios are kept with the run’s records, not in the pull request. It also tidies branches: it deletes a branch whose pull request merged more than a week ago (a few per repository per run), and comments on a pull request closed without merging to record why, leaving that branch in place. Started by core @curate, by schedule, or by a playbook.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The commits and file summaries since its last run, the raw diff, and the current README and documentation.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Diffs and documents go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.

data: Roster name: recon. See also Rule governance.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: Deterministic first: every engine rule is reconciled by code. The model answers only “is this approved free-text rule already implemented by one of these engine rules?” with a rule, none, or unclear. Unclear is preferred to a guess, and it gives no confidence score. Anything it could not read is listed, and the report is marked incomplete. Rule text that tries to dictate the answer is treated as data.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person fixes the rule or the engine, through the four-eyes rule workflow. The reconciler changes neither.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented rules. The board approved “flag any capital purchase line above 750 per unit.” The engine flags at a different threshold. Verdict: Drift, “same unit-price check, at a threshold other than the approved 750.” The engine also runs a check with no rule-book entry: Shadow.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier), for one question only. Everything else is deterministic code.
data.scope#Scope: It reconciles the CapEx engine’s rules. It reconciles rules; it does not score them.
data.what-it-does#What it does: It checks that the business rules your governance board approved are the rules the CapEx engine actually enforces, rule by rule, with citations.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces:
One verdict per rule, each citing what exists: the governance record, the engine rule, or both (a Shadow rule has no governance record; a Missing rule has no engine rule):
Aligned: the engine applies the rule as approved. Drift: same control, different condition or threshold. Shadow: logic runs with no governing rule. A fresh workspace is mostly Shadow, by design. Missing: an approved rule nothing enforces. The report appears in the console, and in the “Rules reconciliation status” issue when that sink is configured.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The tenant’s governance rule book: each rule’s status, the decision behind it, its owners, approved thresholds, and approved free-text new rules. The rules the engine evaluates, with the thresholds it uses and where each is raised.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your Runink TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Rule text goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.

data: Roster name: deployer.
data.guardrails#Guardrails: The request is screened before anything runs; a flagged request produces nothing. The draft, and the release-notes section built from it, are screened by the output guardrails before any pull request opens; a flagged draft opens nothing and the issue says why. Linked pages are reference, not instructions: they are marked as untrusted data, with chat control sequences neutralised. It is instructed to leave out anything that would act on a system or expose one, and to say what it left out. Tags that would start other agents are neutralised in what it posts.
data.human-oversight#Human oversight: A person reviews the pull request and merges, edits or closes it. The deployer never merges, sends no e-mail, and writes only inside your own GitHub organisation. Only your organisation’s own members can start it.
data.illustrative-example#Illustrative exampl: Invented shipment. “@core_deploy face Draft a damage claim to the carrier: 4 of 22 pallets arrived crushed on 28 September, noted on the proof of delivery; damaged value 6,840.00.” TIDE opens a pull request whose release-notes section is the claim letter, citing the delivery date, the noted exception, the four pallets and the amount, and links it on the issue. The coordinator reviews it, merges it, and sends the letter with the photos.
data.model#Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
data.scope#Scope: It drafts from the details given, without looking up records in FACE or PULSE. The draft holds only the facts it was given; check it before sending. It does not execute commands or change systems.
data.what-it-does#What it does:
Describe a task in an issue and tag it @core_deploy; Runink TIDE drafts the result and delivers it as release notes: a pull request in your GitHub organisation that a person reviews and merges. “Deploy” here means “deliver the draft”, not “change a system”.
For FACE: fulfilment, claims and logistics documents, such as a claim letter or a delivery notice. For PULSE: brand, marketing and outreach copy.
data.what-it-produces#What it produces: A pull request that adds a dated section to the top of the release notes (the same file TIDE’s Release Curator maintains) in the repository the issue is in, or in the release-notes repository your organisation designates. The section is the complete deliverable in Markdown, written from the details given; it does not reply with a plan or clarifying questions. A comment on the issue linking the pull request. When the draft reaches the model’s length limit, the section and the pull request title both say it is incomplete. When the pull request cannot be opened, a “not delivered” notice on the issue, and the run fails.
data.what-it-reads#What it reads: The task in the issue, and up to two pages the issue links, as reference only. A linked page is fetched only from websites your deployment has allowed; by default none is.
data.where-it-runs-and-data-handling#Where it: On your TIDE deployment’s own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The task text goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Linked pages are fetched by the agent itself.

data:
Overview is the first page of the Runink TIDE console and the first category on its rail. It answers one question: is anything wrong, and where do I go next? It is a summary, not a second copy of every page. Each line on it links to the page that owns the subject.
This section also covers what you need before you use any other category: how to sign in, how the rail is organised, how the platform is built, and how to read what the console shows you.
Getting startedSign in, choose an instance, and read the Overview page from top to bottom. Console mapEvery rail page, its ?tab= link name, and what it reads. ArchitectureModules, operators, ClientInstance, the security spine, and where the console keeps its data. Status and provenanceHow to read a verdict, an absent value, and a derived figure. Plans and billingTIDE Lite, Dedicated and Enterprise, Compute Units, currency and billing periods. HTTP route referenceEvery route the console registers, and how each class of route is authorised. TroubleshootingSign-in failures and console errors, quoted from the code.
data.what-the-overview-page-does-not-show#Wha:
These sections live on their own pages:
the workload table is on DevEx › Cluster › Namespaces; the instance table is on DevEx › Cluster › Namespaces, on its Instances sub-tab, which is the only instance table; the inference tiers and the model router status are on DataEx › Models & inference; the agent roster is on DataEx › Agents, and the schedules are on DevEx › Agent runs › Runs; the FinOps estimate is on Intelligence › Dashboards, on the CFO Cockpit persona; the data platforms are on DataEx › Connections. The Overview also carries the audit verdict strip: the Platform audit and Model & agent audit verdicts, each with Details, which opens the full audit (checks, actions, history).
data.what-the-overview-page-shows#What the Ov:
From top to bottom:
Section What it reads Refresh Header pill {healthy}/{total} healthy GET /api/dashboard: the Deployments and DaemonSets in the tracked namespaces every 5 s while the tab is visible KPI strip: Client instances, Workloads, Agent runs (7d), Success rate /api/dashboard and GET /api/agent-runs every 5 s Needs attention the open findings of DataEx › Trust › Harness (GET /api/harness), worst first every minute Recent agent runs the eight most recent runs from /api/agent-runs every 5 s Platform one line per subsystem (workloads, instances, inference, data sources from GET /api/connections), each a link to the page that owns it every minute for inference and connections Ask TIDE the orchestration chat, POST /chat when you send The auto-refresh runs only while the Overview tab is on screen. When you return to the tab, it reloads at once instead of showing the numbers you left.

The per-category references give the request and response detail and the exact authorisation of each route:
DevEx, Coding sessions DataEx API reference Intelligence API reference FORGE API reference

data.grpc-web-on-#gRPC-web on \u003ccode\u003:
The root handler serves, in order: gRPC-web (dispatched by content type, so it needs no route of its own), the Flutter bundle from CONSOLE_WEB_DIR, and else the HTML dashboard fallback. The gRPC-web services run in the same process, on the same origin and session, with no CORS: a foreign Origin is refused with 403. They are:
TIDE’s own: CapexService, GovernanceService, WorkspaceService, PlaybookService, ResolveService (an alias of the estate service) and AskService; the shared services TIDE mounts: runink.ui.estate.v1.EstateService, runink.ui.profile.v1.ProfileService, and the datasources ConnectionsService and RunnersService.
data.how-routes-are-authorised#How routes are:
Class Rule Examples Open no session needed /healthz, /api/me, /api/plans Session read a GET needs a signed-in session when sign-in is configured (requireSession); on an open console it is served /api/dashboard, /api/namespaces, /api/gitops Privileged write a session and the adminRefusal predicate against an allowlist env var; audited on success, failure and refusal PUT /api/agent-schedules/{name} (CONSOLE_AGENT_ADMINS), POST /api/connections (CORE_CONNECTION_ADMINS) Machine ingest a shared token generated once in core-system; unset means the door refuses everything POST /api/agent-health (CORE_HEALTH_INGEST_TOKEN), POST /api/rules-recon/report (CORE_RECON_INGEST_TOKEN), POST /api/judgement/submissions (CORE_JUDGEMENT_INGEST_TOKEN) Agent report a GitHub App installation token for the console’s org (authorizeReporter) POST /api/session-runs, POST /api/data-governance-findings, POST /api/judgements, POST /api/playbook-runs/step-report An allowlist that is unset means “every identity this console admits”. That is not a wildcard, because sign-in itself fails closed. CONSOLE_SESSION_ADMINS is the exception: unset means nobody. GET /api/access lists every allowlist. See Trust and access.
Reads that could not reach their source still answer 200, with source: "unavailable" and complete: false in the body. See Status and provenance.
