data: This page explains how Runink TIDE is built: what runs on the cluster, and how trust, data and traffic move through it.
data.clientinstance#ClientInstance:
ClientInstance (core.runink.org/v1alpha1) is the generic tenant instance the platform places on a shared cluster:
Field Meaning app the application identity. Drives the core.runink.org/app label and the dedicated-taint toleration. tenant the tenant key. The core.runink.org/tenant label plus soft node affinity. role controlplane or runner (default runner): selects the PriorityClass. image the container image to run. port the container and service port (default 8080). replicas default 1; ignored when suspend is true. computeUnits a sizing budget, mapped to real CPU and memory limits. It is not the billed Compute Unit (one model-slot second); see Plans and billing. tags client labels added to the pod template and ServiceAccount. placement nodeSelector, tolerations (added to the defaults), affinity (replaces the default soft affinity). env extra environment variables. users access grants: email, role (admin, writer or reader, default reader), optional phone, optional expiresAt. subscription tier (lite, dedicated or enterprise), seats, status (active, suspended or past_due). suspend scale the instance down. Every operator gives each pod the same isolation labels and scheduling: core.runink.org/{app,tenant,role}, runink.org/{app,tenant,role}, the toleration core.runink.org/dedicated=, soft (anti-)affinity and a priorityClassName. Each namespace carries a ResourceQuota, LimitRange, PriorityClass, NetworkPolicy and PodDisruptionBudget.
data.components#Components: Component Role core the single control surface: dev stack, deploys, images, security scans, sessions, the install wizard. See the CLI reference. TIDE console the web console, served by the TIDE operator. Operators one Kubernetes operator each for FACE, PULSE and TIDE’s generic ClientInstance. devgateway the edge: a DaemonSet on host ports 80 and 443 that terminates TLS with a leaf from TIDE’s own CA and routes each host to its frontend. ambassador a small static mTLS TCP proxy. Its image is FROM scratch. modelrouter the one admission queue in front of the inference engines. forgecheck the verifier central CI runs on FORGE projects. core-runner the self-hosted data-access runner.
data.images#Images:
core build builds local podman images only. The images the cluster runs are built in the cluster (werf and buildah in an ephemeral Job) and pushed to the node-local registry. Every Dockerfile pins its base image by @sha256: digest, and the base images are mirrored with core images mirror.
After a delivery roll, workloads run a digest-pinned :latest@sha256:…. A bare kubectl rollout restart then restarts onto the same digest. To move a workload onto new images, run the delivery workflow for that image.
data.inference#Inference: The model plane is sovereign: no hosted model is called. mistral.rs is the engine. The model router is the one admission queue in front of the engines. Budgets across the agents derive from one configured decode rate, INFERENCE_DECODE_TOK_S. See Models and inference.
data.networking#Networking: Manifests work on IPv6 single-stack, IPv4 single-stack and dual-stack clusters: services bind [::], and no Service is pinned to one address family.
data.traffic-the-edge-and-the-apps#Traffic: t:
Each app’s web UI is served by its own small frontend, which serves the Flutter bundle and reverse-proxies gRPC-web, /auth/* and /api/* to the backend. The devgateway edge routes / on each host to that frontend.
The devgateway has its own sign-in gate. When edge auth is on, an empty DEVGW_AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS refuses every sign-in. Admitting any verified Google account needs the explicit DEVGW_AUTH_ALLOW_ANY_VERIFIED=true. Edge sessions are kept server-side.
FORGE runs inside the TIDE console (FORGE › Studio is a console route), on TIDE’s session.
data.trust-defence-in-depth#Trust: defence in:
Everything internal is authenticated and encrypted.
PKI. Every workload holds a short-lived ECDSA leaf signed by the shared cluster CA, and internal connections use mutual TLS. core mesh ca mints and distributes that CA. Encryption at rest. Envelope encryption (AES-GCM) is applied by the object store and the connection store, always. Anything that opens either store needs CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK and refuses to start without it. The object store. TIDE runs its own S3-compatible objectd, which verifies SigV4. The TIDE operator mints every objectd key as a Secret in the consumer’s namespace. App databases. FACE and PULSE seal database values per column before they are written.
data.what-runs-on-the-cluster#What runs on th: Deployments use k0s with pure kustomize overlays (no Helm). The operators are the authoritative source of each pod’s spec and environment.
data.what-tide-is-and-what-it-is-not#What TID:
TIDE is the shared platform for the Runink applications (FACE, PULSE and LUNA), and FORGE is one of its own console categories. Platform concerns live here: self-healing, the event mesh, secrets, the object store, inference serving, MCP, PKI and mTLS, telemetry, the Kubernetes operators and the infrastructure as code.
The apps do not import TIDE. Code that more than one app runs lives in a shared library that TIDE and the apps both import.
data.where-the-console-keeps-its-data#Where t:
The console keeps its metadata in its own encrypted root:
on objectd, when OBJECTSTORE_ENDPOINT and both credentials are set. If objectd is configured but cannot be opened, the console fails closed instead of falling back; otherwise in a local encrypted directory, CONSOLE_APPFS_DIR (default /var/lib/core/appfs), on its persistent volume. Each store (agent health, schedules, runs, lineage, governance findings, judgements, rules reconciliation, session commands and runs, GitHub config, cloud providers, connections, subscriptions) is a table in that root. The audit chain is a hash chain that continues across restarts, and GET /api/audit/verify walks it.
The console republishes the few settings the agents read after every change, so change them in the console: an edit made anywhere else is replaced on the next write.

data:
Runink TIDE is sold on its own, separately from FACE and PULSE. FORGE is part of TIDE: a TIDE plan includes it. Every product has the same three plan categories, and the category says where the work runs, which decides how compute is charged.
The price list is served by the console at GET /api/plans?product=core, which needs no sign-in.
data.compute-units#Compute Units:
1 CU is one second of a model slot, so 3,600 CU is one slot-hour. A slot is one request’s hold on the shared model plane. CU is charged only on Lite, where the work runs on Runink’s hardware. Dedicated and Enterprise are unmetered: their compute runs on your own infrastructure.
On Lite Rule Allowance 18,000 CU a seat a month (5 slot-hours), pooled across the subscription’s seats Over the allowance pay as you go at $0.10 per 100 CU, billed per started block of 100 CU Prepaid CU bought in advance for a month at 10% off, or for a year at 20% off. Unused prepaid CU lapses at the end of its period. Prepaid CU extends a Lite allowance only Fair use at most 900 CU a seat in any rolling hour (15 slot-minutes). Work past that queues: it is never refused and never billed extra
data.cu-is-not-speccomputeunits#CU is not \u0: ClientInstance.spec.computeUnits is a sizing budget for an instance’s pod, not the billed unit: the operator maps it to bounded CPU and memory limits. The FinOps view on Intelligence › Dashboards (CFO Cockpit) multiplies that allocation by the $0.10 per 100 CU rate and labels the result cu-estimate with measure: allocation: it is showback of what was allocated, an estimate, never a charge, and never the metered usage the Billing page shows.
data.currency-and-billing-periods#Currency an: One list, in US dollars. /api/plans and the /api/checkout quote are in US cents. Your regional currency. Billing converts the list into the currency of the purchaser’s country with the European Central Bank’s euro reference rates. The rate is the one in force when the month opens: the last ECB publication before the 1st, fixed for the whole month. Seat prices round to a whole unit of the local currency; usage lines and fees round to its minor unit (cents). A country without a mapped currency is billed in US dollars. A missing or stale rate stops the bill. It is never billed as 0 and never at another rate. Anniversary periods. A period runs from the day of the month your subscription started, 00:00 UTC, to the same day the next month. A start on the 31st bills to the last day of a shorter month (February 28, or 29 in a leap year), then returns to the 31st.
data.how-cu-is-measured#How CU is measured:
The model router (see Models and inference) is the one place that sees both when a request was given a slot on the model plane and when its response finished, so it is the one meter. It measures how long each request held its slot; the time a request spent waiting for a slot is never billed. Billing sums the period’s slot time and converts it to CU once, rounding up, so a period with any usage at all bills at least 1 CU.
Controls on that path:
The router never charges anyone. It measures; it does not know who pays. Metering never blocks a request. If a measurement cannot reach the caller (for example, the client disconnected mid-stream), the request still completes and the gap is counted. A missing measurement records nothing: never a guessed figure. One rule for every product. FACE and TIDE record and read compute units with the same shared recorder and meter, so a slot-second costs the same CU in both. Who pays for the console’s own model calls (Ask TIDE, the grounded Ask, the console chat, and voice transcription). By default, the signed-in person’s purchaser: their own subscription, or the subscription their seat is on. This is the same account the Billing page shows, so every person’s usage lands on the allowance they see. A single-purchaser installation can instead bill every call to one account, whoever asked. Unattributed usage. A call with no signed-in person, or from a person with no subscription and no seat, is counted as unattributed. It stays visible in the console’s metering counters, and it is never invoiced to anyone. Unmeasured sites are listed below. An unmeasured site records nothing; it is never estimated. Each product is metered separately. A TIDE subscription’s Billing page counts only TIDE’s usage (the console and FORGE). A purchaser’s FACE or PULSE usage counts against that product’s own allowance and is never pooled into TIDE’s. The Billing page shows given against used for the current anniversary period: the plan’s CU allowance, the CU measured so far, and the period’s start and end. With no current period on record, the page says compute units are not measured rather than showing a lifetime total. An app instance TIDE runs for a subscriber (FACE, PULSE) shows the same period on its own Billing page; an instance with no period on record shows usage as unmeasured. Platform work is never billed. TIDE’s own agents on their own triggers (the reviewer, fixer, curator and the rest, on a schedule, a pull request or a mention) are never metered. Agents a person dispatches are billed to that person’s purchaser. A Trust › Harness dispatch, or an Atlas playbook run a person started, carries a short-lived billing grant; the purchaser’s identity stays in the console and never reaches the Git host. A retried report is never counted twice, and a grant cannot record more time than the run could have used. A run nobody attributable started (a schedule, an event-triggered playbook, a person with no TIDE subscription or seat) is unmeasured: never billed to anyone.
data.seats-subscriptions-and-the-billing-page: Seats are managed on the instance’s Admin page, through the billing seat routes (/api/billing/seats). Nobody changes their own access, the last admin stays, and a full seat pool refuses an invite. See Trust and access. One subscription per email. Every route that starts a checkout (/api/signup, /api/checkout and the Billing page) refuses a second subscription for the same purchaser. The public signup is gated by reCAPTCHA when it is configured. Checkout goes through Stripe, and only when the installation configures it. Without it the quote still works and the page says billing is not configured. A Dedicated plan can name its cloud account at checkout (cloudTenant: a GCP project, a Databricks workspace or a Snowflake account). A Lite plan naming one is refused, because Lite runs on shared hardware and has no runners of its own. Entitlement fails closed. A subscription is entitled only while it is active, trialing or past due; anything else, an unknown plan, or an unreadable subscription record grants no plan, never Lite and never a free tier. The Billing page (opened from Account) is the shared billing component. It shows a usage figure only where a meter feeds it: an unmeasured value is shown as unmeasured, never as zero, and an estimate is never shown as a charge. For where TIDE can deploy a runner, and what a connected runner does, see Runners.
data.the-three-categories#The three categorie:
TIDE Lite TIDE Dedicated TIDE Enterprise Where the work runs Runink’s shared hardware, spot-style runners in your own cloud account: GCP, Databricks or Snowflake your premises (on-prem runners) or your own cloud account Priced per seat (a person), 1–9 seats node (a machine), from 1 node custom quote Price $75 a seat a month billed yearly, or $89 a seat month to month $249 a month for the first node, then $149 a month for each extra node; yearly contract custom Compute 18,000 CU a seat a month, metered unlimited CU, on your own cloud bill unlimited CU Other charges CU over the allowance (below) 1% of the runners’ cloud cost none on on-prem runners There is no node fee and no flat platform fee on any plan: the plan’s platformMonthlyCents is 0. On-prem runners are Enterprise only. A yearly price is charged as twelve times the monthly rate.
The seat or node count must fit the plan’s band, or the quote is refused with the band’s minSeats and maxSeats. A Dedicated plan offered month to month is refused with “this plan is annual-only; retry with annual=true”. Enterprise returns no quote: /api/checkout answers custom: true and directs you to sales.

data: This page takes you from the sign-in screen to a first reading of the Overview page. It describes the console as the code in this repository builds it.
data.next-steps#Next steps: Find any page: Console map Understand the pieces: Architecture Read verdicts correctly: Status and provenance Operate the platform: DevEx Connect data: DataEx
data.step-1-sign-in#Step 1: sign in:
The console offers the sign-in methods that are configured. GET /api/me tells the web app which ones to show (googleAuth, passwordAuth, authRequired).
Method Turned on by Notes Google GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID The ID token is verified locally against the issuer’s keys. The issuer is https://accounts.google.com unless OIDC_ISSUER overrides it. The email must be verified. Username and password CONSOLE_ADMIN_PASSWORD The user name is CONSOLE_ADMIN_USERNAME, default admin. Compared in constant time. reCAPTCHA (optional) RECAPTCHA_SITE_KEY, RECAPTCHA_API_KEY and a project id Checked before the credential when all three are set. Who may sign in is decided by CONSOLE_ALLOWED_EMAILS (a list) or CONSOLE_ALLOWED_HD (a hosted domain). When neither is set, every Google sign-in is refused. The check fails closed on purpose.
If neither GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID nor CONSOLE_ADMIN_PASSWORD is set, the console runs open: no sign-in screen, every read works. Privileged writes are then refused, because nobody can be named in the audit trail. Each refusal says so, for example “this console has no sign-in configured, so an Atlas CapEx change would be unattributable”. Sessions are server-side. The cookie core_console_session holds an opaque session id; the session itself lives in the console’s own encrypted store and lasts 12 hours. Log out (/auth/logout) revokes it on the server.
data.step-2-choose-an-instance#Step 2: choose:
After sign-in the console shows landing cards: one per instance (ClientInstance) you hold a live grant on, read from the shared profile service. Choosing one tells the console which instance to act for. The choice is kept in the browser (or in ?instance=), and the server is never told: every admin call names the instance and is checked again on the server.
You can continue without an instance. A ?tab= deep link also skips the landing cards.
The Admin row sits in the rail footer, under the instance row, and appears only when the server reports that you are an admin of the chosen instance. This is a display rule only: every access call checks the role again.
data.step-3-learn-the-rail#Step 3: learn the:
The rail has five categories, in this order:
Category Question it answers Overview Is anything wrong, and where do I go next? DevEx What the cluster runs and how traffic reaches it, whether it runs what was delivered, what the agents did and found, and whether the record of every action is intact. DataEx Which models serve, which agents act and under what limits, which sources TIDE reads and what reads them, and who may do what. Intelligence What the platform knows about the data estate: its quality through each reader’s lens (Overview), the sources and how data flows (Estate), CapEx, the rules and the playbooks. FORGE What is being built: FORGE’s chats, opened in the Studio. The instance row, Admin (for an admin of that instance), Account and Log out are in the rail footer. The rail has 16 rows. Below a window width of 720 px, the rail moves into a drawer. See the console map for every page.
Every page can be linked with ?tab=, for example /?tab=gitops. There is one route, and the URL does not change as you move around. An unknown name opens Overview; a retired name opens the page that now owns its subject.
data.step-4-read-the-overview-page#Step 4: re:
Read it from top to bottom:
The header. The pill says {healthy}/{total} healthy for the workloads the console tracks (Deployments and DaemonSets in core-system, runink-system, pulse-system, luna-system, inference-system, github-runners and registry-system). The header also names its source (kube-api) and the time of the data. If the dashboard read failed, a red notice gives the reason and the source is marked absent. The KPI strip. Client instances (ready and not suspended, out of all), Workloads (healthy out of total), Agent runs (7d) and Success rate. An empty instance list is shown as neutral, not green: nothing to judge is not a pass. Needs attention. The open findings from Trust › Harness, worst first, each with a link to act on it. Recent agent runs. The eight newest runs, with the freshness of the run store stated above them. Platform. One line each for workloads, instances, inference and data sources, each linking to its page. Ask TIDE. The orchestration chat (see below). The agent-run tiles need the TIDE GitHub App. Without it they show “—” and the sentence “Install the TIDE GitHub App to show agent-run status + logs here. It needs actions:read; the console mints a short-lived installation token itself.” That is a missing configuration, not zero runs. The Success rate is success ÷ (success + failure). Runs that are still running or were cancelled count in the total but not in the rate. When no run has finished, the tile shows “—”.
data.step-5-ask-tide#Step 5: ask TIDE:
The chat box sends POST /chat {"message": "..."}. The console’s model turns the sentence into exactly one tool call:
read tools such as list_client_instances and reply run at once; the one mutating tool, create_client_instance, is proposed, not run. You get the exact action and arguments back with a one-time code, and nothing happens until you send confirm . The code is bound to you, single-use, and expires after 5 minutes. The CONSOLE_INSTANCE_ADMINS allowlist is checked again when you confirm. What you type, and what the model answers, pass through the console’s guardrail before the model sees the input and before you see the output. A blocked message returns 403 with the guardrail’s wording.
The speaker and microphone buttons appear only when the voice services are wired: TTSD_URL for speech output and VOICE_REMOTE_URL for speech input (reported as voiceTts and voiceStt by /api/me).
data.where-the-console-runs#Where the console:
The Runink TIDE console is not a separate service. It is an HTTP server inside the TIDE operator process, on every replica. It serves:
the Flutter web app from CONSOLE_WEB_DIR (with an HTML fallback page when that is unset); the JSON API under /api/* and the sign-in routes under /auth/*; gRPC-web for the Atlas, Ask and shared-UI services, on the same origin and the same session. TIDE is deployed per client installation, so each installation has its own console URL. The CLI has no default console URL for the same reason: --console-url (or CORE_CONSOLE_URL) is set per installation.

data: The console is built around one rule: it never shows a health or a number that nobody measured. This page explains how that rule appears on screen and in the API, so you can tell healthy from not measured, and a measured figure from a derived one.
data.not-measured-is-a-real-answer#Not measur:
Many endpoints distinguish nothing found from could not look. Read the difference, because the fix is different:
Where Not measured looks like It does not mean Report endpoints (/api/compliance, /api/governance, …) source: "unavailable", complete: false, entries in unmeasured[] an empty estate DevEx › GitOps drift: null when neither the desired nor the running version was read no drift Live CPU and memory a 403 from the kubelet proxy is reported as unmeasured zero usage Connector probe (/api/connectors/status) never probed: “NOT MEASURED” down Data governance agent a source nobody explored in Resolve is UNASSESSABLE compliant Judge agent unable-to-judge, with the reason agreement Ask (Intelligence, DataEx) COULD_NOT_LOOK FOUND_NOTHING
data.the-api-convention-behind-it#The API con:
Every report endpoint on the console follows one convention:
A report GET that could not read its source answers 200 with source: "unavailable" and complete: false. It does not answer 503. A 503, then, means the console (or the edge in front of it) did not answer. That is a different fact. The web client has one ladder: 401 sends you back to sign in; any other non-200 is an error. The reasons are in the code: a 503 is what the edge emits when the console is down, so the two would be indistinguishable; a 503 tells intermediaries to retry a condition that no retry can fix; and a non-200 would throw away the gap report the body carries.
The CRUD routes (/api/connections and its siblings) are not reports, and may answer 503 when the registry cannot be written.
data.the-metrics-page#The Metrics page:
DevEx › Metrics reads GET /api/metrics. It reports only what the console process can measure:
process: goroutines, heapBytes, sysBytes, gcCycles, cpus, gomaxprocs, uptimeSecs, goVersion, and on Linux openFDs and rssBytes (source: "runtime"); workloads: the tracked Deployments and DaemonSets, with total, degraded and complete (source: "kube-api"); utilisation: live CPU and memory, from metrics.k8s.io when it exists, else from the kubelet Summary API through the API server’s node proxy (labelled kubelet-summary). It lists what it does not measure in unmeasured: an availability SLO (it needs a Prometheus time series), network throughput (it needs node interface counters), and per-tenant ClientInstance workloads (the panel covers the platform namespaces only). There is no uptime percentage on the page, because nothing measures one.
data.three-kinds-of-value#Three kinds of valu:
Each value on a page carries a provenance, drawn next to its source:
Provenance Meaning Example measured read from its source on this refresh the Overview header’s kube-api source when the dashboard read succeeded derived computed from measured values, not observed directly the Overview Success rate: success ÷ (success + failure) absent could not be read; the reason is shown instead of a value the header’s source when /api/dashboard returned an error An absent value is never drawn as zero, empty or green.
data.time#Time: Timestamps belong to the data, not to your browser. A page header’s “as of” time is parsed from the payload (for example generated in /api/dashboard), not stamped with the current time. Agent run rows show the run’s own timestamp in the same format, prefixed with the date when it was not the same day. The console does not compute “3m ago” from the browser clock, so a stale history never looks fresh.
data.verdicts#Verdicts:
A page that was built for an endpoint which had no page opens on a status indicator: one dot, one headline, the source and the time, and an explicit absent form with the reason. Tones run from ok, info and neutral to warn and danger.
Green is earned. An empty list has nothing to judge, so it is neutral, not a pass. For example, the Client instances tile is neutral when there are no instances, green only when every instance is ready, and amber otherwise.

data: Problems with signing in, with the edge in front of the console, and with reading the Overview. Each message is quoted from the code, so you can search for it. For other areas see the troubleshooting page of DevEx, DataEx, Intelligence and FORGE.
data.-is-not-authorized-for-this-console#\u00:
Cause. The Google account signed in correctly, but it is not on the console’s allowlist. When neither CONSOLE_ALLOWED_EMAILS nor CONSOLE_ALLOWED_HD is set, every Google sign-in is refused. This is deliberate: the allowlist fails closed.
Fix. Add the address to CONSOLE_ALLOWED_EMAILS (a list) or set CONSOLE_ALLOWED_HD to your hosted domain. The name is CONSOLE_ALLOWED_EMAILS, not the apps’ AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS.
data.-is-not-permitted-to--on-this-console-co: The shape is is not permitted to on this console (). You are signed in, but a privileged write checks a named allowlist and you are not on it. The name in brackets is the one to change: CONSOLE_AGENT_ADMINS, CORE_CONNECTION_ADMINS, CONSOLE_INSTANCE_ADMINS, CORE_ATLAS_ADMINS, CORE_RUNNER_ADMINS or CONSOLE_SESSION_ADMINS. data.sign-in-failed-try-again--error-sign-in-: The Google ID token did not verify: a wrong audience (the console’s GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID), a wrong issuer (OIDC_ISSUER, default https://accounts.google.com), or an unverified email.
data.sign-in-is-unavailable-this-console-cann:
Cause. Sessions are stored server-side in the console’s encrypted appfs root, and it cannot be mounted. At boot the console logs 🛑 CONSOLE SIGN-IN DISABLED — a sign-in method is configured but the session store (appfs core-console/run/sessions) cannot be mounted, so every sign-in will be refused. It does not exit, because the same process also reconciles the fleet.
Fix. Check CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK and the OBJECTSTORE_* or CONSOLE_APPFS_DIR wiring of the core-operator Deployment. The mount is retried on the next sign-in.
data.sign-out-could-not-revoke-your-session-o: A 503 from /auth/logout: the session store could not be written. The session still expires after its 12-hour lifetime.
data.the-edge-devgateway#The edge (devgateway:
These come from the edge’s sign-in gate, in front of every routed host.
Message Cause Fix auth: is not permitted (403) the account is not on the edge allowlist add it to the edge’s allowlist auth: sign-in is unavailable (no session store) — tell an operator (503) the edge’s session store is not mounted see the boot log line below auth: state expired (400) the sign-in round trip took too long start the sign-in again auth: token exchange failed (502) the OIDC token exchange with the identity provider failed check the edge log line auth: token exchange failed: … At boot, the edge logs its configuration errors as ERROR: edge auth is ENABLED but …:
… DEVGW_AUTH_ALLOWED_EMAILS is empty — every sign-in will be REFUSED. Populate the edge’s allowlist, or set DEVGW_AUTH_ALLOW_ANY_VERIFIED=true to admit any verified Google account on purpose. … DEVGW_SESSION_KEY is unset or shorter than 16 bytes …. Provide the edge’s session key (identical on every edge pod) and roll the DaemonSet. … the session store cannot be mounted …. Set CORE_ENVELOPE_KEK and either OBJECTSTORE_* or a writable DEVGW_APPFS_DIR, then roll the DaemonSet. The edge stays up in every one of these cases and keeps serving /healthz. It terminates TLS for every routed host, so crash-looping it would turn a sign-in outage into a total one.
